questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A patient can feel sustained pressure but cannot detect a pinprick, an excessively hot surface, or histamine-induced itching in a patch of skin. Which receptor type is most directly impaired?

options.text: Free nerve endings
Merkel cell-neurite complexes
Meissner corpuscles
Lamellated (Pacinian) corpuscles

questions.explanation: Free nerve endings extend through the papillary dermis into lower epidermal layers and are the principal cutaneous receptors for pain, temperature extremes, and itching. They can also contribute to crude touch.

distractorExplanations.B: Merkel complexes are tonic mechanoreceptors for sustained light touch and texture, not the principal receptors for pain, temperature, and itch.
distractorExplanations.C: Meissner corpuscles are encapsulated phasic receptors for light touch and low-frequency deformation.
distractorExplanations.D: Pacinian corpuscles are deep encapsulated receptors for coarse pressure and high-frequency vibration.

questions.learningObjective: Associate free nerve endings with pain, temperature, itching, and crude tactile input.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Epidermal free nerve endings detect pain, temperature extremes, itching, and mechanical movements of the skin.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which receptor-location-function combination best identifies the tonic receptor that continues signaling while a small object presses against the skin?

options.text: Merkel cell-neurite complex in the stratum basale; sustained light touch and texture
Meissner corpuscle in the hypodermis; high-frequency vibration
Pacinian corpuscle in the epidermis; pain and temperature
Root hair plexus in glabrous skin; sustained deep pressure

acceptedFreeText: Merkel cell-neurite complex in the stratum basale; sustained light touch and texture
questions.explanation: Merkel cells lie in the basal epidermis and contact expanded sensory axon endings. Their tonic response preserves information about sustained light touch and surface texture.

distractorExplanations.B: Meissner corpuscles lie in dermal papillae and respond rapidly to light touch or low-frequency deformation.
distractorExplanations.C: Pacinian corpuscles are deep in reticular dermis or hypodermis and detect pressure and high-frequency vibration.
distractorExplanations.D: Root hair plexuses surround hair follicles in hairy skin and respond to hair movement.

questions.learningObjective: Identify Merkel complexes by their basal epidermal location and tonic texture-sensing function.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Merkel cells with expanded axonal endings are tonic receptors for sustained light touch and object texture.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A small elliptical encapsulated receptor located inside a dermal papilla of a fingertip is most specialized for which sensory input?

options.text: Light touch and low-frequency skin deformation
Sustained tissue stretch and torque
High-frequency vibration and deep pressure
Pain, temperature extremes, and itching

acceptedFreeText: Light touch and low-frequency skin deformation
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles occupy dermal papillae, especially in fingertips, palms, and soles. They are rapidly responding encapsulated mechanoreceptors for light touch and low-frequency deformation.

distractorExplanations.B: Ruffini corpuscles detect stretch, tension, and twisting of tissue.
distractorExplanations.C: Pacinian corpuscles detect high-frequency vibration and deeper pressure.
distractorExplanations.D: Free nerve endings are the main receptors for pain, temperature extremes, and itch.

questions.learningObjective: Match Meissner corpuscles with dermal papillae, glabrous skin, and light-touch input.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae detect light touch and low-frequency stimuli and are numerous in fingertips, palms, and soles.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which receptor is preferentially activated by a high-frequency vibrating instrument pressed firmly against the skin?

options.text: Merkel cell-neurite complex
Root hair plexus
Lamellated (Pacinian) corpuscle
Free nerve ending

questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are large, deeply located, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors whose concentric lamellae transmit changes in coarse pressure and high-frequency vibration to the central axon.

distractorExplanations.A: Merkel complexes encode sustained light touch and texture in the basal epidermis.
distractorExplanations.B: Root hair plexuses detect displacement of hairs rather than deep high-frequency vibration.
distractorExplanations.D: Free nerve endings mainly signal pain, temperature, itch, and some crude touch.

questions.learningObjective: Associate Pacinian corpuscles with deep pressure and high-frequency vibration.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Lamellated Pacinian corpuscles detect coarse touch, pressure, and high-frequency vibration.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A small ovoid encapsulated receptor in the skin of the glans penis or clitoris is described in Junqueira as responding primarily to what?

options.text: Low-frequency vibration or movement
High-frequency vibration and deep pressure
Sustained texture discrimination
Noxious heat and itching

questions.explanation: Krause end bulbs are simple encapsulated ovoid receptors found mainly in genital skin and are described as sensing low-frequency vibration or movement.

distractorExplanations.B: High-frequency vibration and deep pressure are characteristic of Pacinian corpuscles.
distractorExplanations.C: Sustained texture discrimination is characteristic of Merkel cell-neurite complexes.
distractorExplanations.D: Noxious temperature and itch are detected mainly by free nerve endings.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the location and tested modality of Krause end bulbs.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Krause end bulbs are found primarily in penile and clitoral skin and sense low-frequency vibrations.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A fusiform encapsulated receptor is firmly anchored to surrounding dermal connective tissue. Deformation of its collagenous capsule most directly signals which stimulus?

options.text: Skin stretch, tension, or twisting
Hair movement
Pinprick and burning pain
Fine low-force texture at the basal epidermis

questions.explanation: Ruffini corpuscles have fusiform collagenous capsules anchored to connective tissue. Stretch or torque distorts the capsule and stimulates the sensory axon.

distractorExplanations.B: Hair movement is detected by a root hair plexus.
distractorExplanations.C: Pain is detected mainly by free nerve endings.
distractorExplanations.D: Sustained light touch and texture at the basal epidermis are detected by Merkel complexes.

questions.learningObjective: Associate Ruffini corpuscles with tissue stretch, tension, and torque.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Ruffini corpuscles have fusiform collagenous capsules and detect tissue distortion, stretch, or twisting.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A slight breeze bends hairs on the forearm without appreciably indenting the skin. Which receptor transduces this movement most directly?

options.text: Root hair plexus
Pacinian corpuscle
Merkel cell-neurite complex
Krause end bulb

questions.explanation: The root hair plexus is an unencapsulated web of sensory fibers around the base of a hair follicle in the reticular dermis. Bending the hair deforms these endings and produces a light-touch signal.

distractorExplanations.B: Pacinian corpuscles respond to deeper pressure and high-frequency vibration.
distractorExplanations.C: Merkel complexes respond tonically to direct sustained touch and texture.
distractorExplanations.D: Krause end bulbs are encapsulated genital receptors for low-frequency vibration.

questions.learningObjective: Identify root hair plexuses as receptors for hair displacement in hairy skin.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Root hair plexuses surround hair-follicle bases in the reticular dermis and detect hair movement.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A histology section shows a 100-micrometer elliptical structure within a dermal papilla. Flattened modified Schwann cells form stacked transverse layers around winding sensory axons. What is it?

options.text: Meissner corpuscle
Pacinian corpuscle
Ruffini corpuscle
Root hair plexus

questions.explanation: The superficial dermal-papilla location and stacked flattened Schwann cells oriented roughly perpendicular to the epidermis are the classic recognition clues for a Meissner tactile corpuscle.

distractorExplanations.B: A Pacinian corpuscle is much larger, deep, and onion-like with many concentric lamellae.
distractorExplanations.C: A Ruffini corpuscle is fusiform with a collagenous capsule anchored to surrounding tissue.
distractorExplanations.D: A root hair plexus is an unencapsulated web around a hair follicle rather than an oval corpuscle in a dermal papilla.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize Meissner corpuscles by microscopic architecture and superficial location.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Meissner corpuscles are elliptical structures in dermal papillae containing axons among stacked flattened Schwann cells.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A large oval receptor among adipocytes in the hypodermis contains 15-50 concentric lamellae surrounding a central axon. Which structure is shown?

options.text: Merkel cell-neurite complex
Meissner corpuscle
Lamellated (Pacinian) corpuscle
Free nerve ending

questions.explanation: The deep location, large size, and onion-like concentric lamellae of modified Schwann cells are diagnostic of a Pacinian corpuscle.

distractorExplanations.A: A Merkel complex is microscopic and unencapsulated in the stratum basale.
distractorExplanations.B: A Meissner corpuscle is smaller and superficial, with stacked layers inside a dermal papilla rather than concentric onion-like lamellae.
distractorExplanations.D: A free nerve ending lacks a capsule and cannot form this large lamellated structure.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize Pacinian corpuscles by their onion-like lamellae and deep location.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Pacinian corpuscles are large deep oval structures with 15-50 concentric lamellae around an axonal core.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which group contains only unencapsulated cutaneous sensory receptors?

options.text: Free nerve endings, Merkel tactile discs, and root hair plexuses
Meissner, Pacinian, and Ruffini corpuscles
Merkel tactile discs, Meissner corpuscles, and Krause end bulbs
Free nerve endings, Pacinian corpuscles, and root hair plexuses

acceptedFreeText: Free nerve endings, Merkel tactile discs, and root hair plexuses
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings, Merkel-associated tactile discs, and root hair plexuses lack connective-tissue capsules. Meissner, Pacinian, Krause, and Ruffini receptors are encapsulated.

distractorExplanations.B: All three listed structures are encapsulated receptors.
distractorExplanations.C: Meissner corpuscles and Krause end bulbs are encapsulated.
distractorExplanations.D: Pacinian corpuscles possess a conspicuous multilamellar capsule.

questions.learningObjective: Classify cutaneous receptors as encapsulated or unencapsulated.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Free endings, Merkel discs, and root hair plexuses are unencapsulated; Meissner, Pacinian, Krause, and Ruffini receptors are encapsulated.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A receptor continues to discharge while a textured object remains stationary against the skin, whereas another responds strongly when light contact first deforms the skin and then adapts rapidly. Which pair best matches these responses?

options.text: Merkel complex first; Meissner corpuscle second
Meissner corpuscle first; Merkel complex second
Pacinian corpuscle first; free nerve ending second
Root hair plexus first; Ruffini corpuscle second

acceptedFreeText: Merkel complex first; Meissner corpuscle second
questions.explanation: Merkel complexes are tonic receptors that preserve information during sustained light touch. Meissner corpuscles are encapsulated phasic mechanoreceptors that respond rapidly to changing light-touch deformation.

distractorExplanations.B: This reverses the adaptation patterns: Merkel is tonic and Meissner is phasic.
distractorExplanations.C: Pacinian corpuscles are phasic high-frequency and pressure receptors, while free endings mainly signal pain, temperature, itch, and crude touch.
distractorExplanations.D: Root hair plexuses emphasize hair movement; this pair does not provide the classic tonic sustained-texture versus phasic light-touch contrast.

questions.learningObjective: Use tonic versus phasic behavior to distinguish Merkel and Meissner receptors.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Merkel complexes are tonic receptors; encapsulated receptors such as Meissner corpuscles respond rapidly to mechanical change.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: An age-related decline in which receptor helps explain worsening two-point discrimination at the fingertips?

options.text: Meissner corpuscles
Pacinian corpuscles
Free nerve endings
Ruffini corpuscles

questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles are densely represented in fingertips and support fine spatial discrimination of light touch. Junqueira notes that their density declines during adult life and can be estimated by two-point discrimination testing.

distractorExplanations.B: Pacinian corpuscles primarily detect deep pressure and high-frequency vibration, not fine superficial two-point discrimination.
distractorExplanations.C: Free nerve endings primarily mediate pain, temperature, itch, and crude tactile input.
distractorExplanations.D: Ruffini corpuscles primarily detect stretch and torque.

questions.learningObjective: Connect fingertip two-point discrimination with Meissner corpuscle density.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: Meissner corpuscle density can be estimated by two-point discrimination and normally declines during adult life.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which superficial-to-deep sequence of cutaneous receptors is correct?

options.text: Merkel complex in basal epidermis -> Meissner corpuscle in dermal papilla -> Pacinian corpuscle in deep reticular dermis or hypodermis
Pacinian corpuscle in basal epidermis -> Merkel complex in dermal papilla -> Meissner corpuscle in hypodermis
Meissner corpuscle in stratum corneum -> Pacinian corpuscle in papillary dermis -> Merkel complex in hypodermis
Ruffini corpuscle in epidermis -> free nerve ending only in hypodermis -> Merkel complex around a hair bulb

acceptedFreeText: Merkel complex in basal epidermis -> Meissner corpuscle in dermal papilla -> Pacinian corpuscle in deep reticular dermis or hypodermis
questions.explanation: Merkel complexes are epidermal, Meissner corpuscles occupy superficial dermal papillae, and the large Pacinian corpuscles lie deep in reticular dermis or subcutaneous tissue.

distractorExplanations.B: All three structures are assigned to the wrong depths.
distractorExplanations.C: Meissner corpuscles are not in the stratum corneum, and Merkel complexes are not hypodermal.
distractorExplanations.D: Ruffini corpuscles are encapsulated dermal receptors; free endings extend into superficial skin; Merkel cells occupy the basal epidermis.

questions.learningObjective: Map the principal cutaneous mechanoreceptors from epidermis to hypodermis.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.excerpt: The receptor map places Merkel discs in basal epidermis, Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae, and Pacinian corpuscles deep in dermis or hypodermis.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which two sensory structures may extend into or reside within the epidermis rather than forming encapsulated corpuscles in the dermis?

options.text: Free nerve endings and Merkel-associated tactile discs
Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles
Ruffini corpuscles and Krause end bulbs
Root hair plexuses and Pacinian corpuscles

distractorExplanations.B: Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles are encapsulated and lie in dermis or hypodermis.
distractorExplanations.C: Ruffini corpuscles and Krause end bulbs are encapsulated dermal receptors.
distractorExplanations.D: Root hair plexuses surround follicles in the reticular dermis, while Pacinian corpuscles lie deep.

source.excerpt: The epidermis contains free nerve endings and Merkel-associated tactile discs, both with unencapsulated nerve fibers.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A light-microscopy stain shows a basement membrane beneath an epithelium. Which statement best distinguishes it from the basal lamina?

options.text: The basement membrane includes the epithelial basal lamina plus an underlying reticular lamina
The basement membrane is only the lamina lucida, whereas the basal lamina is only the lamina densa
The basal lamina is made by fibroblasts, whereas the basement membrane is made only by epithelial cells
The terms describe two unrelated structures on opposite surfaces of an epithelial cell

questions.explanation: The basal lamina is an epithelial extracellular-matrix layer; the light-microscopic basement membrane includes it together with the connective-tissue reticular lamina.

distractorExplanations.B: Lamina lucida and lamina densa are subdivisions associated with the basal lamina, not the stated distinction.
distractorExplanations.C: The production relationship is reversed and oversimplified: epithelial cells contribute basal-lamina components, while connective-tissue cells contribute the reticular lamina.
distractorExplanations.D: Both structures are at the basal interface and are closely related.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate basal lamina from the light-microscopic basement membrane.

questions.prompt: Which molecular linkage most directly connects the zonula adherens of one epithelial cell to the actin cytoskeleton of its neighbor?

options.text: Cadherins linked intracellularly through catenins to actin filaments
Connexins assembled into connexons and linked to microtubules
Integrins linked through plakins to intermediate filaments
Claudins and occludins linked directly to keratin filaments

questions.explanation: In a zonula adherens, transmembrane cadherins bind across the intercellular space and catenins connect them to cortical actin.

distractorExplanations.B: Connexins form gap junction channels, not adherens junctions.
distractorExplanations.C: Integrin–intermediate filament linkage describes a hemidesmosome at the basal surface.
distractorExplanations.D: Claudins and occludins are characteristic of tight junctions; they do not form the adherens belt.

questions.prompt: A gap-junction channel spanning two adjacent epithelial cells is formed by the alignment of two connexons. What is each connexon?

options.text: A hexamer of connexin proteins
A tetramer of claudin proteins
A pair of cadherin dimers
A ring of six integrin heterodimers

questions.explanation: Each hemichannel, or connexon, is assembled from six connexin subunits; connexons in adjacent cells align to form the communicating channel.

distractorExplanations.B: Claudins form sealing strands in tight junctions.
distractorExplanations.C: Cadherins mediate adhesion but do not form the aqueous gap-junction pore.
distractorExplanations.D: Integrins mediate cell–matrix adhesion rather than forming intercellular channels.

Within the gland lumen; they propel secretion by motile cilia
In the surrounding connective tissue; they synthesize the reticular lamina
At the apical surface of acinar cells; they seal the lumen with tight junctions

Central multilobed nucleus with fine neutral granules
Kidney-shaped nucleus with abundant lysosomes and pseudopodia
Round central nucleus surrounded by a single large lipid droplet

questions.prompt: In an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, which event most directly triggers mast-cell degranulation?

options.text: Cross-linking of FcεRI-bound IgE by a multivalent antigen
Binding of IgG to collagen type I fibrils
Phagocytosis of an erythrocyte through Fcγ receptors
Recognition of antigen by a plasma-cell surface immunoglobulin

questions.explanation: Antigen cross-links IgE already bound to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on the mast-cell surface, initiating release of histamine and other mediators.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly follows collagen synthesis from the fibroblast to formation of an extracellular fibril?

options.text: Hydroxylation and glycosylation → procollagen triple helix → secretion → cleavage of terminal propeptides → fibril assembly
Terminal-propeptide cleavage in rough ER → secretion of tropocollagen → hydroxylation outside the cell → fibril assembly
Triple-helix formation in the Golgi → extracellular glycosylation → secretion → intracellular cross-linking
Fibril assembly in secretory vesicles → exocytosis → conversion of collagen to procollagen outside the cell

questions.explanation: Pro-α chains are hydroxylated and glycosylated in the cell, assemble as procollagen, and are secreted. Extracellular procollagen peptidases remove terminal propeptides, allowing tropocollagen fibril assembly and cross-linking.

distractorExplanations.B: Propeptide cleavage is extracellular, whereas hydroxylation occurs intracellularly before secretion.
distractorExplanations.C: Triple-helix formation begins in the rough ER, and glycosylation is not solely extracellular.
distractorExplanations.D: Fibrils do not normally assemble within secretory vesicles; procollagen is the secreted soluble precursor.

questions.learningObjective: Order the intracellular and extracellular stages of collagen fibril formation.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which description correctly relates a glycosaminoglycan (GAG), a proteoglycan monomer, and a proteoglycan aggregate?

options.text: GAG chains attach to a core protein to form a proteoglycan monomer; many monomers can bind a hyaluronan backbone
A core protein attaches to collagen to form a GAG; many GAGs then make hyaluronan
Hyaluronan is covalently attached to every core protein and is itself a sulfated GAG
Proteoglycan aggregates are formed only from fibronectin and laminin without carbohydrate chains

questions.explanation: Most proteoglycan monomers consist of sulfated GAG chains on a core protein. Large aggregates form when many monomers associate noncovalently with a hyaluronan backbone via link proteins.

distractorExplanations.B: The hierarchy is reversed: GAG chains are carbohydrate components of proteoglycans.
distractorExplanations.C: Hyaluronan is nonsulfated and generally serves as the long backbone through noncovalent interactions.
distractorExplanations.D: Fibronectin and laminin are adhesive glycoproteins, not the sole components of proteoglycan aggregates.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish GAGs, proteoglycan monomers, and proteoglycan aggregates.

Perikaryal cytoplasm around the nucleus
Proximal dendritic cytoplasm
Regions containing rough endoplasmic reticulum

questions.explanation: Nissl substance represents rough ER and free polyribosomes. It is present in the soma and dendrites but absent from the axon hillock and axon.

distractorExplanations.B: The soma contains abundant Nissl substance.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of axonal transport direction and motor protein is correct?

options.text: Kinesin: anterograde toward the terminal; dynein: retrograde toward the soma
Dynein: anterograde toward the terminal; kinesin: retrograde toward the soma
Kinesin: both directions along actin; myosin: retrograde along microtubules
Myosin: anterograde along microtubules; dynein: both directions along actin

questions.explanation: Microtubule-based kinesin generally carries cargo anterogradely toward the axon terminal, whereas cytoplasmic dynein mediates retrograde transport toward the cell body.

distractorExplanations.B: The motors are reversed.
distractorExplanations.C: Fast axonal transport is chiefly microtubule-based, not a kinesin-on-actin system.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which structural feature provides the principal diffusion barrier of the blood–brain barrier?

options.text: Continuous capillary endothelial cells joined by tight junctions
Fenestrated capillary endothelial cells covered only by astrocyte processes
A continuous layer of ependymal cells around every CNS capillary
Pericytes joined by gap junctions that completely replace endothelial junctions

questions.explanation: The core barrier is the nonfenestrated continuous endothelium sealed by tight junctions. Its basal lamina, pericytes, and astrocytic end-feet support and regulate the barrier but do not replace the endothelial seal.

distractorExplanations.B: CNS capillaries are characteristically nonfenestrated, and astrocyte end-feet are supportive rather than the primary seal.
distractorExplanations.C: Ependymal cells line ventricles and the central canal, not every capillary.
distractorExplanations.D: Pericytes contribute to barrier regulation, but endothelial tight junctions are the principal diffusion barrier.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which mapping of connective-tissue sheath to peripheral-nerve structure is correct?

options.text: Endoneurium surrounds individual nerve fibers; perineurium surrounds fascicles; epineurium surrounds the whole nerve
Endoneurium surrounds fascicles; perineurium surrounds the whole nerve; epineurium surrounds individual axons
Perineurium surrounds individual fibers; endoneurium surrounds fascicles; epineurium surrounds nodes of Ranvier
Epineurium surrounds individual Schwann cells; perineurium surrounds myelin lamellae; endoneurium surrounds the whole nerve

questions.explanation: Endoneurium is the delicate connective tissue around individual fibers, perineurium forms the cellular sheath of each fascicle, and epineurium encloses and binds the entire nerve.

distractorExplanations.B: This reverses all three levels.
distractorExplanations.C: The perineurium belongs around fascicles, not individual fibers.
distractorExplanations.D: Myelin is produced by Schwann cells; these connective-tissue sheaths are not arranged as stated.

questions.learningObjective: Map endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium to their anatomical levels.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts interstitial and appositional growth of cartilage?

options.text: Interstitial growth results from division of chondrocytes within the matrix; appositional growth results from chondrogenic cells in the perichondrium adding tissue at the surface
Interstitial growth occurs only from perichondrial osteoblasts; appositional growth occurs from isogenous groups deep in cartilage
Both mechanisms require blood vessels to enter lacunae and directly supply dividing chondrocytes
Appositional growth is the only mechanism in articular cartilage because it has a thick perichondrium

questions.explanation: Interstitial growth expands cartilage from within through chondrocyte division and matrix secretion. Appositional growth adds cartilage at the surface from chondrogenic cells of the perichondrium.

distractorExplanations.B: The cellular sources are reversed.
distractorExplanations.C: Cartilage is avascular; chondrocytes receive nutrients by diffusion.
distractorExplanations.D: Articular cartilage lacks a perichondrium, so it cannot grow appositionally from that source.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate interstitial from appositional cartilage growth.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which combination is most characteristic of fibrocartilage?

options.text: Thick bundles of type I collagen, chondrocytes in rows, and no perichondrium
A glassy matrix rich in type II collagen, isogenous groups, and a perichondrium at every surface
A dense network of elastic fibers and a mineralized perichondrium
Type IV collagen sheets surrounding adipocytes and abundant fenestrated capillaries

questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage combines features of dense connective tissue and cartilage: prominent type I collagen bundles, chondrocytes often aligned in rows, and absence of perichondrium.

distractorExplanations.B: This is closer to hyaline cartilage, and articular hyaline cartilage still lacks perichondrium.
distractorExplanations.C: Elastic cartilage has elastic fibers but is not characterized by a mineralized perichondrium.
distractorExplanations.D: Type IV collagen forms basal laminae, not the principal matrix of fibrocartilage.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the matrix and covering features of fibrocartilage.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which feature best distinguishes Volkmann canals from Haversian canals in compact bone?

options.text: Volkmann canals run transversely or obliquely, connect osteonal canals, and are not surrounded by concentric lamellae
Volkmann canals lie at the center of every osteon and are surrounded by concentric lamellae
Volkmann canals contain only osteocytes, whereas Haversian canals contain only marrow
Volkmann canals are microscopic channels between lacunae through which osteocyte processes pass

questions.explanation: Haversian canals run longitudinally at osteon centers and are surrounded by concentric lamellae. Volkmann canals cross between them and are not themselves centers of osteons.

distractorExplanations.B: This describes a Haversian canal.
distractorExplanations.C: Both canal types carry vessels and nerves; neither is defined by containing only osteocytes or marrow.
distractorExplanations.D: Canaliculi, not Volkmann canals, connect lacunae and contain osteocyte processes.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish perforating Volkmann canals from central Haversian canals.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes the two principal synovial-lining cell types?

options.text: Type A cells are macrophage-like and phagocytic; type B cells are fibroblast-like and synthesize hyaluronan and other matrix components
Type A cells secrete immunoglobulin; type B cells resorb bone with a ruffled border
Type A cells produce myelin; type B cells form the articular cartilage perichondrium
Type A cells are endothelial; type B cells are smooth-muscle cells that pump synovial fluid

questions.explanation: Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-derived phagocytic cells. Type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like secretory cells that contribute hyaluronan and lubricating components to synovial fluid.

distractorExplanations.B: These functions describe plasma cells and osteoclasts, not synoviocytes.
distractorExplanations.C: Synoviocytes neither myelinate nerves nor create a perichondrium over articular cartilage.
distractorExplanations.D: The synovial intima is not an endothelial–smooth muscle pump.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Keratinocyte lamellar granules contribute most directly to which epidermal function?

options.text: Formation of the extracellular lipid water barrier in the stratum granulosum
Synthesis of melanin in the stratum basale
Antigen presentation by Langerhans cells
Anchoring the epidermis to the reticular dermis with type I collagen

questions.explanation: Lamellar granules release lipid-rich contents between cells of the upper granular layer, helping create the permeability barrier that limits transepidermal water loss.

distractorExplanations.B: Melanin is synthesized in melanocytes, not in keratinocyte lamellar granules.
distractorExplanations.C: Langerhans cells perform antigen presentation.
distractorExplanations.D: Type I collagen is a major dermal matrix component; the epidermal attachment involves the basement-membrane zone.

questions.prompt: Which epidermal cell pairing of origin and usual location is correct?

Melanocyte: bone marrow, mainly stratum corneum; Langerhans cell: neural crest, mainly stratum basale
Merkel cell: mesoderm, mainly stratum granulosum; keratinocyte: neural crest, mainly dermis
Langerhans cell: epidermal ectoderm, mainly stratum lucidum; melanocyte: endoderm, mainly dermis

questions.explanation: Melanocytes derive from neural crest and occupy the basal layer. Langerhans cells are bone-marrow-derived antigen-presenting cells found mainly among spinous-layer keratinocytes.

questions.prompt: A skin specimen has a very thick stratum corneum and a distinct stratum lucidum. Which additional finding should be expected?

Numerous hair follicles and sebaceous glands but no sweat glands
A thin epidermis with no dermal papillae
Apocrine glands opening directly onto the surface throughout the specimen

questions.explanation: Thick skin of palms and soles has a thick epidermis with stratum lucidum and abundant eccrine sweat glands, but it lacks hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the major vascular plexuses of the skin?

options.text: A deep plexus lies near the dermis–hypodermis junction, and a superficial plexus lies in the papillary region and supplies capillary loops
The epidermis contains a dense superficial plexus, while the dermis is avascular
Both plexuses are confined to the stratum basale and directly contact keratinocytes
A superficial arterial plexus lies in the stratum corneum, and a deep venous plexus lies inside hair shafts

questions.explanation: The avascular epidermis is nourished by diffusion from dermal vessels. A deep cutaneous plexus is near the dermis–hypodermis boundary, and a superficial/subpapillary plexus sends capillary loops into dermal papillae.

Intracellular sodium for extracellular potassium
Intracellular calcium for extracellular magnesium
Intracellular hydrogen for extracellular sodium

HbA: β4; HbA2: γ4; HbF: α4

questions.prompt: Which platelet structure–content pairing is correct?

Central granulomere: hemoglobin; alpha granules: histamine only; dense granules: collagen type I
Peripheral hyalomere: nucleus and rough ER; alpha granules: DNA; dense granules: myelin basic protein
Open canalicular system: actin-free lipid droplets; alpha granules: bile salts; dense granules: thyroxine

Primary granules contain hemoglobin; secondary granules contain immunoglobulin
Primary granules contain histamine and heparin; secondary granules contain major basic protein
Primary granules contain insulin; secondary granules contain collagen type II

options.text: Woven (immature) bone
Compact (cortical) bone

questions.explanation: Irregular newly deposited matrix with haphazard collagen and numerous osteocytes, often near an ossification front, identifies woven immature bone.

distractorExplanations.B: Mature compact bone has orderly parallel or concentric lamellae and well-formed osteons.
distractorExplanations.C: Spongy describes trabecular architecture; mature trabeculae can be lamellar, whereas woven describes matrix maturity.
distractorExplanations.D: Hyaline cartilage has chondrocytes in a homogeneous avascular matrix rather than osteoid and bone-forming surfaces.

questions.prompt: Identify the tissue or dominant lining pattern in this unfamiliar microscope field. Write the most specific practical answer.

options.text: Compact (cortical) bone
Spongy (cancellous) bone
Hyaline cartilage
Woven (immature) bone

questions.explanation: Irregular newly deposited matrix with haphazard collagen and numerous osteocytes, often near an ossification front, identifies woven immature bone.

distractorExplanations.A: Mature compact bone has orderly parallel or concentric lamellae and well-formed osteons.
distractorExplanations.B: Spongy describes trabecular architecture; mature trabeculae can be lamellar, whereas woven describes matrix maturity.
distractorExplanations.C: Hyaline cartilage has chondrocytes in a homogeneous avascular matrix rather than osteoid and bone-forming surfaces.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Identify the tissue or dominant lining pattern in this unfamiliar microscope field. Write the most specific practical answer.

options.text: Peripheral nerve
Sensory (dorsal root) ganglion
White adipose tissue
Tendon

questions.explanation: Wavy longitudinal axons or round myelin-cleared profiles are grouped into fascicles surrounded by perineurium and epineurium; neuronal somata are absent.

distractorExplanations.B: A sensory ganglion contains conspicuous large neuronal cell bodies ringed by satellite cells.
distractorExplanations.C: Fat cells are much larger, form a honeycomb sheet and have flattened peripheral nuclei rather than many tiny myelin rings.
distractorExplanations.D: Tendon shows parallel eosinophilic collagen bundles and rows of flattened tenocyte nuclei, not fascicles enclosed by perineurium.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize Peripheral nerve across unfamiliar stains, species, fields and magnifications, and distinguish its closest Aug 22 practical look-alikes.

distractorExplanations.D: Tendon is mostly parallel collagen with sparse flattened nuclei and has no striated branching cells.

Ligament

distractorExplanations.C: Skeletal muscle has cellular fibers, peripheral nuclei and striations rather than mostly extracellular collagen.
distractorExplanations.D: Nerve shows axons, Schwann-cell nuclei and a perineurial boundary rather than uniformly eosinophilic collagen bundles.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Identify the tissue or dominant lining pattern in this unfamiliar microscope field. Write the most specific practical answer.

options.text: Ligament
Tendon
Fibrocartilage
Peripheral nerve

questions.explanation: Dense collagen bundles connect bone to bone and may blend into fibrocartilage at an enthesis. An isolated dense-regular H&E field can be impossible to distinguish reliably from tendon; attachment context or elastic-fiber content is then required.

distractorExplanations.B: Tendon is usually more uniformly parallel with highly regular rows of elongated tenocytes and connects muscle to bone, but an isolated H&E field without attachment context may not be conclusive.
distractorExplanations.C: Fibrocartilage has true chondrocytes in lacunae between collagen bundles; ligament proper has fibroblast nuclei without lacunae.
distractorExplanations.D: A nerve has fascicles bounded by perineurium and many axon profiles, not dense collagen bundles alone.

options.text: Thin skin (hair-bearing skin)
Thick skin (glabrous skin)
Pseudostratified epithelium
Transitional epithelium

questions.explanation: A relatively thin epidermis with a modest stratum corneum plus hair follicles and sebaceous glands identifies thin, hair-bearing skin.

distractorExplanations.B: Thick skin has a massive stratum corneum, prominent ridges and no hair follicles or sebaceous glands.
distractorExplanations.C: Pseudostratified epithelium has nuclei at different heights but every cell contacts the basement membrane; it does not keratinize.
distractorExplanations.D: Urothelium has rounded umbrella cells and variable thickness but no keratin sheet or dermal appendages.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Identify the tissue or dominant lining pattern in this unfamiliar microscope field. Write the most specific practical answer.

options.text: Simple cuboidal epithelium
Transitional epithelium (urothelium)
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium

questions.explanation: A single layer of cells about as tall as they are wide surrounds a lumen, with round central nuclei. High-yield sites include renal tubules, thyroid follicles, small ducts and the ovarian surface.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: The intensely magenta apical material in the intestinal goblet cells is best explained by which staining reaction?

options.text: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) reaction for carbohydrate-rich glycoproteins
Orcein staining of elastic fibers
Silver impregnation of reticular fibers
Masson trichrome staining of collagen

questions.explanation: PAS oxidizes carbohydrate groups and produces a magenta reaction product. Mucins and the glycocalyx of intestinal epithelium are therefore strongly PAS-positive.

distractorExplanations.B: Orcein highlights elastic fibers, not carbohydrate-rich mucin.
distractorExplanations.C: Silver methods typically render reticular fibers dark or black.
distractorExplanations.D: Masson trichrome distinguishes collagen from muscle but does not produce this selective magenta mucin pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize PAS-positive mucosubstances in an intestinal section.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.chapter: Chapter 1 - Histology and Its Methods of Study

media.alt: PAS-stained small-intestinal epithelium with magenta goblet-cell mucin

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: The delicate branching black network surrounding cells in this section is composed mainly of which structure?

options.text: Type I collagen bundles
Type III collagen reticular fibers
Elastin lamellae
Keratin intermediate filaments

questions.explanation: Argyrophilic reticular fibers are composed predominantly of type III collagen. Silver impregnation makes their fine branching network appear black.

distractorExplanations.A: Type I collagen forms thicker bundles and is better demonstrated with stains such as trichrome.
distractorExplanations.C: Elastic fibers are classically highlighted by orcein or aldehyde fuchsin.
distractorExplanations.D: Keratin is intracellular and is usually detected immunohistochemically.

questions.learningObjective: Identify silver-stained reticular fibers and recall their collagen type.

media.alt: Silver-stained branching reticular fiber network

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which tissue is shown, with chondrocytes in lacunae, isogenous groups, and a smooth basophilic matrix?

options.text: Hyaline cartilage
Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Compact bone

questions.explanation: Hyaline cartilage has a glassy type II collagen-rich matrix, lacunae containing chondrocytes, and frequent isogenous groups. A perichondrium is present at the edge in this field.

distractorExplanations.B: Elastic cartilage would show a conspicuous network of elastic fibers in the matrix.
distractorExplanations.C: Fibrocartilage has rows of chondrocytes between thick eosinophilic type I collagen bundles and lacks a perichondrium.
distractorExplanations.D: Compact bone contains lamellae, osteons, and canaliculi rather than this homogeneous cartilage matrix.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize hyaline cartilage on routine light microscopy.

media.alt: Hyaline cartilage showing lacunae and isogenous chondrocyte groups

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Rows of chondrocytes lie between thick eosinophilic collagen bundles in this tissue. What is it?

options.text: Hyaline cartilage
Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Dense irregular connective tissue

questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage combines chondrocytes in lacunae with prominent type I collagen bundles, often arranging the cells in rows. It lacks a distinct perichondrium.

distractorExplanations.A: Hyaline cartilage has a more homogeneous, glassy matrix without obvious thick collagen bundles.
distractorExplanations.B: Elastic cartilage contains branching elastic fibers and usually a perichondrium.
distractorExplanations.D: Dense irregular connective tissue lacks chondrocytes enclosed in lacunae.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish fibrocartilage from other cartilage and dense connective tissues.

media.alt: Fibrocartilage with rows of chondrocytes among collagen bundles

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: What structural unit is centered on the dark canal in this compact bone field?

options.text: Trabecula
Osteon (Haversian system)
Epiphyseal plate
Perichondrium

questions.explanation: An osteon consists of concentric lamellae arranged around a central Haversian canal. Osteocyte lacunae and radiating canaliculi are distributed between the lamellae.

distractorExplanations.A: A trabecula is a plate or strut of cancellous bone and is not organized around a central canal this way.
distractorExplanations.C: An epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage organized into zones of chondrocyte maturation.
distractorExplanations.D: Perichondrium surrounds most cartilage and is not a unit of compact bone.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize an osteon and its defining concentric organization.

media.alt: Ground compact bone showing an osteon around a central canal

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which muscle type is shown by branching striated fibers with centrally placed nuclei?

options.text: Skeletal muscle
Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Dense regular connective tissue

questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are striated, branch, and usually contain one central nucleus. Cell boundaries may show intercalated discs.

distractorExplanations.A: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, parallel, unbranched, and multinucleated with peripheral nuclei.
distractorExplanations.C: Smooth muscle lacks cross-striations and has spindle-shaped cells.
distractorExplanations.D: Dense regular connective tissue shows parallel collagen bundles with sparse fibroblast nuclei, not striated cells.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate cardiac muscle from skeletal and smooth muscle in an H&E section.

media.alt: Cardiac muscle with branching striated fibers and central nuclei

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Which leukocyte is identified by its bilobed nucleus and numerous coarse eosinophilic granules?

options.text: Neutrophil
Eosinophil
Basophil
Monocyte

questions.explanation: Eosinophils characteristically have a bilobed nucleus and abundant large specific granules that stain pink-red with eosin.

distractorExplanations.A: Neutrophils typically have three to five nuclear lobes and finer, paler specific granules.
distractorExplanations.C: Basophils have dark basophilic granules that often obscure the nucleus.
distractorExplanations.D: Monocytes have a kidney-shaped nucleus and gray-blue cytoplasm without coarse eosinophilic granules.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize an eosinophil in a peripheral blood smear.

media.alt: Blood smear showing an eosinophil with bilobed nucleus and coarse granules

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: This lobulated lymphoid organ has dark peripheral cortex and pale central medulla in each lobule. Which organ is it?

options.text: Thymus
Lymph node
Spleen
Palatine tonsil

questions.explanation: The thymus is divided into lobules with densely basophilic cortex and lighter medulla. Medullary Hassall corpuscles are another distinctive feature.

distractorExplanations.B: Lymph nodes have cortex with follicles and a medulla with cords and sinuses, not repeated cortex-medulla lobules.
distractorExplanations.C: Spleen has white pulp scattered within red pulp and lacks cortex-medulla lobulation.
distractorExplanations.D: Palatine tonsil has surface stratified squamous epithelium and deep crypts.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the lobular cortex-medulla organization of thymus.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology
source.chapter: Chapter 14 - The Immune System and Lymphoid Organs

media.alt: Adult thymus showing lobules with dark cortex and pale medulla

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A lymphoid nodule surrounds an eccentrically placed central arteriole and is embedded in red pulp. Which organ is shown?

options.text: Thymus
Lymph node
Spleen
Appendix

questions.explanation: Splenic white pulp consists of lymphoid tissue organized around central arterioles and surrounded by red pulp containing sinusoids and cords.

distractorExplanations.A: Thymus has cortex-medulla lobules and no lymphoid follicles or central arterioles.
distractorExplanations.B: A lymph node has subcapsular and medullary sinuses but no red pulp.
distractorExplanations.D: Appendix has intestinal mucosa and abundant lymphoid follicles in its wall, not splenic red pulp.

questions.learningObjective: Identify splenic white pulp and its relationship to a central arteriole.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: The image places primordial germ cells temporarily in the yolk-sac wall near the allantois. Where must these cells migrate to establish the future gonads?

options.text: Genital ridges on the posterior abdominal wall
Surface ectoderm of the genital tubercle
Septum transversum
Neural tube

acceptedFreeText: Genital ridges on the posterior abdominal wall
questions.explanation: Primordial germ cells are first identifiable in the yolk-sac wall near the allantois. They migrate along the dorsal mesentery of the hindgut to the genital or gonadal ridges, where they populate the developing gonads.

distractorExplanations.B: External genital ectoderm is not the destination of primordial germ-cell migration.
distractorExplanations.C: The septum transversum contributes to diaphragm and liver-associated structures, not the germ-cell destination.
distractorExplanations.D: The neural tube does not receive primordial germ cells.

questions.learningObjective: Trace primordial germ cells from the yolk-sac wall to the gonadal ridges.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: This low-power field is dominated by branching eosinophilic trabeculae separated by marrow spaces rather than concentric osteons. Which tissue is being shown?

options.text: Compact lamellar bone
Spongy or cancellous bone
Hyaline cartilage
Dense regular connective tissue

questions.explanation: Spongy bone is organized as a three-dimensional network of trabeculae with intervening marrow spaces. Compact bone instead forms dense lamellae arranged around Haversian canals as osteons.

distractorExplanations.A: Compact bone is dense and typically displays osteons rather than broad interconnected marrow spaces.
distractorExplanations.C: Hyaline cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae within a glassy matrix, not trabeculae around marrow.
distractorExplanations.D: Dense regular connective tissue forms parallel collagen bundles without mineralized trabeculae.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish cancellous bone from compact bone and cartilage at low magnification.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: The low-power field shows opposing articular surfaces separated by a true joint cavity and surrounded by a capsule. Which class of joint is this?

options.text: Fibrous suture
Primary cartilaginous joint
Secondary cartilaginous joint
Synovial joint

questions.explanation: A synovial joint has a real cavity between articular surfaces, hyaline articular cartilage, a fibrous capsule, and an inner synovial lining. Fibrous and cartilaginous joints do not contain a synovial cavity.

distractorExplanations.A: A fibrous suture joins bones with dense connective tissue and has no joint cavity.
distractorExplanations.B: A synchondrosis is united by hyaline cartilage without a synovial space.
distractorExplanations.C: A symphysis is united by fibrocartilage and lacks a true synovial cavity.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a synovial joint from its low-power architecture.

questions.subtopic: Lymphatic drainage — tracheobronchial nodes and bronchomediastinal trunks
questions.prompt: Lymph from the lungs passes through tracheobronchial nodes. Efferent vessels ascending from these nodes contribute to which lymphatic trunks?

options.text: Jugular trunks
Lumbar trunks
Bronchomediastinal trunks
Subclavian trunks

questions.explanation: Tracheobronchial efferents ascend along the trachea and join vessels from other thoracic nodes to form the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks.

distractorExplanations.A: The named efferent trunks in this pulmonary pathway are bronchomediastinal, not jugular.
distractorExplanations.B: Lumbar trunks are not the thoracic efferent trunks formed by this lung drainage pathway.
distractorExplanations.D: Subclavian trunks are not the named continuation of tracheobronchial efferents in this pathway.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A lesion of a nerve formed from C3–C5 weakens contraction of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Which nerve has been injured?

options.text: Phrenic nerve
Vagus nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
An intercostal nerve

questions.explanation: The diaphragm receives motor supply from the phrenic nerve, formed from C3–C5. Diaphragmatic contraction normally flattens its dome and increases thoracic volume.

distractorExplanations.B: The vagus is not the C3–C5 motor nerve supplying the diaphragm.
distractorExplanations.C: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies laryngeal muscles rather than the hemidiaphragm.
distractorExplanations.D: Intercostal nerves supply the thoracic wall; the diaphragm’s motor supply is phrenic.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why examination of the posterior lower chest is important when assessing the inferior lobe of the right lung?

options.text: The right middle lobe covers nearly the entire posterior chest
The right superior lobe extends inferiorly over the whole diaphragmatic surface
The three right lung lobes have equal posterior surface areas
The costal surface of the inferior lobe lies against the posterior and inferior thoracic wall

questions.explanation: The inferior lobe has a large costal surface against the posterior and inferior walls; the middle lobe lies mainly against the lower anterior and lateral wall.

distractorExplanations.A: The middle lobe is predominantly anterior and lateral, not the main lobe covering the posterior lower chest.
distractorExplanations.B: The superior lobe is mainly related to the upper anterolateral wall and apex, not the whole inferior surface.
distractorExplanations.C: The lobes have unequal surface relationships; the inferior lobe is particularly prominent posteriorly.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: The suprapleural membrane supports the cervical pleura at the thoracic inlet. Which pair describes its principal bony attachments?

options.text: Clavicle and transverse process of C3
Medial margin of rib 1 and transverse process of C7
Medial margin of rib 12 and transverse process of C7
Xiphoid process and transverse process of T12

questions.explanation: The suprapleural membrane attaches laterally to the medial first-rib margin and posteriorly to the C7 transverse process, supporting the cervical pleural dome.

distractorExplanations.A: The membrane is anchored to rib 1 and C7, not the clavicle and C3.
distractorExplanations.C: Rib 12 is at the inferior thorax and is not an attachment of this membrane over the lung apex.
distractorExplanations.D: These are inferior thoracic landmarks, not the attachments of the membrane at the superior thoracic aperture.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers destined for glands of the nasal mucosa travel in the greater petrosal nerve. Where do these fibers synapse before postganglionic fibers accompany branches of V2?

options.text: Pterygopalatine ganglion
Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion
Trigeminal ganglion
Inferior vagal ganglion

questions.explanation: Greater petrosal fibers from the facial nerve synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Postganglionic fibers then accompany maxillary nerve branches to the glands.

distractorExplanations.B: The superior cervical ganglion is the synaptic site for the sympathetic pathway, not this parasympathetic pathway.
distractorExplanations.C: V2 branches distribute the postganglionic fibers, but the parasympathetic synapse is not in the trigeminal sensory ganglion.
distractorExplanations.D: The inferior vagal ganglion is not the relay for facial greater-petrosal secretomotor fibers to nasal glands.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the pterygopalatine ganglion in the nasal secretomotor pathway.

Axillary nodes
Tracheobronchial nodes
Retropharyngeal and upper deep cervical nodes

questions.explanation: Posterior nasal lymph drains toward retropharyngeal and upper deep cervical nodes. Anterior nasal lymph may pass forward onto the face toward submandibular nodes.

distractorExplanations.A: The submandibular pathway is associated with anterior nasal regions and does not describe the posterior route asked about.
distractorExplanations.B: Axillary nodes do not receive the principal posterior nasal drainage shown in these sources.
distractorExplanations.C: Tracheobronchial nodes are associated with pulmonary drainage, not the posterior nasal cavity.

options.text: Superior thyroid artery
Inferior thyroid artery
Facial artery
Ascending pharyngeal artery

questions.explanation: The inferior laryngeal artery is a branch of the inferior thyroid artery, which arises from the thyrocervical trunk.

distractorExplanations.A: The superior thyroid artery gives rise to the superior laryngeal artery, not the inferior laryngeal artery.
distractorExplanations.C: The facial artery contributes to pharyngeal and tonsillar supply but is not the parent of the inferior laryngeal artery.
distractorExplanations.D: The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the pharynx but is not the parent vessel specified here.

questions.prompt: Lymphatics from laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds pass toward deep cervical nodes near the carotid bifurcation. Which artery do they accompany?

Lingual artery
Superior laryngeal artery
Superior labial artery

questions.explanation: Lymphatics above the vocal folds follow the superior laryngeal artery to deep cervical nodes associated with the common carotid bifurcation.

distractorExplanations.B: The lingual artery is not the artery followed by the supraglottic drainage pathway described here.
distractorExplanations.D: The superior labial artery is not part of this laryngeal lymphatic route.

questions.prompt: An endoscope is used to examine the natural drainage opening of the maxillary sinus. In which nasal passage should this opening be sought?

Middle nasal meatus
Superior nasal meatus
Spheno-ethmoidal recess

questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus opens high on its medial wall into the semilunar hiatus of the middle nasal meatus.

distractorExplanations.A: The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct, not the natural maxillary sinus opening.
distractorExplanations.C: The posterior ethmoidal cells open into the superior meatus.
distractorExplanations.D: This recess receives the sphenoidal sinus, not the maxillary sinus.

questions.prompt: A clinician follows the natural opening of the sphenoidal sinus into the nasal cavity. Where does the opening lead?

options.text: Middle nasal meatus
Spheno-ethmoidal recess
Inferior nasal meatus
Nasopharyngeal opening of the auditory tube

questions.explanation: The sphenoidal sinus opens onto the posterior roof of the nasal cavity in the spheno-ethmoidal recess.

distractorExplanations.A: The middle meatus receives frontal, maxillary, and anterior or middle ethmoidal drainage.
distractorExplanations.C: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.

questions.prompt: Excess tears enter the nose through the nasolacrimal duct. The duct opens beneath which nasal concha?

options.text: Inferior nasal concha
Middle nasal concha
Superior nasal concha
No concha; it opens directly into the nasopharynx

questions.explanation: The duct opens into the inferior nasal meatus beneath the anterior lip of the inferior concha.

distractorExplanations.B: The middle meatus beneath this concha receives several paranasal sinus openings, not the nasolacrimal duct.
distractorExplanations.C: The superior meatus is associated with posterior ethmoidal drainage.
distractorExplanations.D: The duct opens on the lateral nasal wall, not directly into the nasopharynx.

questions.prompt: Infection is confined to the posterior ethmoidal air cells. Which nasal passage receives their usual drainage?

options.text: Inferior nasal meatus
Semilunar hiatus in the middle meatus
Spheno-ethmoidal recess
Superior nasal meatus

questions.explanation: Posterior ethmoidal cells usually open onto the lateral wall of the superior nasal meatus.

distractorExplanations.A: This meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct.
distractorExplanations.B: The semilunar hiatus is associated with maxillary and anterior sinus drainage, not the usual posterior ethmoidal openings.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: After a fracture involving the roof of the nasal cavity, a patient loses the sense of smell. Which structure normally transmits the injured olfactory axons into the cranial cavity?

options.text: Foramen rotundum
Incisive canal
Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
Sphenopalatine foramen

questions.explanation: Bundles of olfactory receptor axons pass through small cribriform plate perforations to reach the olfactory bulb.

distractorExplanations.A: Foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve; it is not the route of olfactory axons.
distractorExplanations.B: The incisive canal connects the nasal floor and oral palate and carries the nasopalatine nerve and vessels.
distractorExplanations.D: This connects the pterygopalatine fossa and nasal cavity and transmits nasal neurovascular branches.

Inferior concha and lacrimal bone
Palatine process of the maxilla and horizontal plate of the palatine
Nasal bone and zygomatic bone

questions.explanation: The posterior septum is formed mainly by the vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid; septal cartilage is anterior.

distractorExplanations.B: These contribute to the lateral nasal wall rather than most of the septum.
distractorExplanations.C: These form the hard palate and nasal floor, not the principal vertical posterior septum.
distractorExplanations.D: The nasal bone makes only a small septal contribution, and the zygomatic bone is not a principal septal component.

Inferior nasal concha
Superior nasal concha
Uncinate process

distractorExplanations.A: The middle concha is a process of the ethmoidal labyrinth.
distractorExplanations.C: The superior concha is also part of the ethmoid.
distractorExplanations.D: The uncinate process is an ethmoidal projection and is not a separate nasal concha.

questions.prompt: A patient has bleeding from the common superficial arterial anastomotic area of the nasal septum. Where is this area located?

options.text: Posterior roof over the sphenoidal sinus opening
Anterior region of the medial nasal wall
Lateral wall of the superior nasal meatus
Roof of the nasopharynx over the pharyngeal tonsil

questions.explanation: Superficial anastomoses of greater palatine, sphenopalatine, superior labial, and anterior ethmoidal branches occur on the anterior septum.

distractorExplanations.A: The common superficial septal anastomotic area is anterior, not at the sphenoidal sinus opening.
distractorExplanations.C: This is not the anterior medial-wall anastomotic area described in the question.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve division supplies general sensation to the anterior region of the nasal cavity, chiefly through the anterior ethmoidal nerve?

options.text: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2)
Olfactory nerve (I)
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1)
Facial nerve (VII)

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal nerve is a nasociliary branch of V1; ophthalmic branches supply the anterior nasal region.

distractorExplanations.A: V2 supplies much of the posterior nasal cavity; it is not the parent division of the anterior ethmoidal nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: The olfactory nerve mediates smell, not general sensation.
distractorExplanations.D: Facial parasympathetic fibers provide secretomotor supply to nasal glands, not this general sensory pathway.

Sphenoidal sinus
Posterior ethmoidal cells
Maxillary sinus

Palatopharyngeus
Salpingopharyngeus
Stylopharyngeus

The rima glottidis between the vocal folds
The pharyngeal isthmus between nasopharynx and oropharynx
The tracheal bifurcation

questions.explanation: The elevated soft palate seals against the pharyngeal wall and closes the pharyngeal isthmus, separating the two regions.

External laryngeal nerve
Maxillary nerve (V2)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)

questions.prompt: During a deep inspiration, which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is chiefly responsible for abducting the vocal folds and widening the rima glottidis?

options.text: Lateral crico-arytenoid
Posterior crico-arytenoid
Transverse arytenoid
Cricothyroid

questions.explanation: Posterior crico-arytenoid rotates the arytenoids laterally and abducts the vocal folds, opening the rima glottidis.

distractorExplanations.A: It rotates the arytenoids medially and adducts the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: It draws the arytenoid cartilages together rather than abducting them.
distractorExplanations.D: It lengthens and tensions the vocal folds rather than acting as their primary abductor.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the primary abductor of the vocal folds.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic muscles — posterior crico-arytenoid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.subtopic: Nerves — external laryngeal nerve and cricothyroid
questions.prompt: After a neck operation, a singer has difficulty increasing vocal-fold tension. Injury to the nerve supplying cricothyroid is suspected. Which nerve is this?

options.text: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve

questions.explanation: The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid, whose action lengthens and tensions the vocal folds.

distractorExplanations.A: The internal branch is mainly sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: It supplies the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles, but not cricothyroid.
distractorExplanations.D: IX supplies stylopharyngeus and oropharyngeal sensation, not cricothyroid.

questions.learningObjective: Associate cricothyroid with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — external laryngeal nerve and cricothyroid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A recurrent laryngeal nerve is injured. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle on that side retains its direct motor supply?

options.text: Posterior crico-arytenoid
Lateral crico-arytenoid
Vocalis
Cricothyroid

questions.explanation: Cricothyroid is the intrinsic laryngeal exception: its motor supply is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

distractorExplanations.A: Its direct motor supply is from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: This muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.C: Vocalis receives recurrent laryngeal motor fibers and therefore is not the spared exception.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the intrinsic laryngeal muscle spared by a recurrent laryngeal nerve lesion.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — recurrent laryngeal motor distribution

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.subtopic: Thyrohyoid membrane; nerves — internal laryngeal nerve
questions.prompt: A sensory nerve reaches the larynx by piercing the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery. Which region is mainly supplied by this nerve?

options.text: Laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds only
Skin over the anterior neck
Anterior nasal mucosa
Laryngeal mucosa above the level of the vocal folds

questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and supplies the laryngeal cavity down to vocal-fold level.

distractorExplanations.A: Sensory supply below the folds comes from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the internal laryngeal cavity, not this cutaneous territory.
distractorExplanations.C: Anterior nasal general sensation is supplied by ophthalmic trigeminal branches, especially the anterior ethmoidal nerve.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sensory territory of the internal laryngeal nerve.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Thyrohyoid membrane; nerves — internal laryngeal nerve

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which nerve carries general sensation from the laryngeal cavity below the vocal folds?

options.text: Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is sensory below the vocal folds as well as motor to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

distractorExplanations.A: Its main sensory territory extends from above down to the level of the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: This branch supplies cricothyroid rather than the infraglottic sensory territory.
distractorExplanations.D: IX supplies oropharyngeal sensation, not the infraglottic cavity.

questions.learningObjective: Identify sensory innervation of the infraglottic larynx.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — recurrent laryngeal sensory distribution

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Contraction of cricothyroid pulls the thyroid cartilage forward and tilts it downward relative to the cricoid. What is the principal effect on the vocal ligaments?

options.text: They lengthen and become more tense
They shorten and become less tense
They are abducted primarily by lateral rotation of the arytenoids
They move superiorly to become vestibular ligaments

questions.explanation: Forward and downward thyroid rotation increases the distance between the thyroid angle and arytenoid attachments, lengthening the vocal ligaments.

distractorExplanations.B: This is opposite to the effect of the described cricothyroid movement.
distractorExplanations.C: Primary abduction is produced by posterior crico-arytenoid acting at the crico-arytenoid joints.
distractorExplanations.D: Vocal and vestibular ligaments are distinct structures and do not transform into one another.

questions.learningObjective: Relate cricothyroid joint movement to vocal-fold tension.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Laryngeal joints; cricothyroid action

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which unpaired intrinsic muscle spans between the posterior surfaces of the two arytenoid cartilages and draws them together?

options.text: Transverse arytenoid
Posterior crico-arytenoid
Cricothyroid
Vocalis

questions.explanation: The single transverse arytenoid spans between the arytenoids and adducts the cartilages.

distractorExplanations.B: This paired muscle runs from cricoid to arytenoid and abducts the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: Cricothyroid runs between cricoid and thyroid cartilages and tensions the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.D: Vocalis runs alongside each vocal ligament and adjusts its tension; it does not span between the two arytenoids.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the transverse arytenoid and its action.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic muscles — transverse arytenoid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which intrinsic muscle rotates the arytenoid cartilage medially to adduct a vocal fold?

options.text: Posterior crico-arytenoid
Lateral crico-arytenoid
Cricothyroid
Salpingopharyngeus

questions.explanation: Lateral crico-arytenoid pulls on the muscular process to internally rotate the arytenoid and adduct the vocal fold.

distractorExplanations.A: It produces lateral rotation and abduction, the opposite movement.
distractorExplanations.C: It mainly lengthens the vocal fold through the cricothyroid joint.
distractorExplanations.D: This is a longitudinal pharyngeal muscle, not an intrinsic muscle acting on the arytenoid.

questions.learningObjective: Link lateral crico-arytenoid action to closure of the vocal folds.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic muscles — lateral crico-arytenoid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: The thickened free upper margin of the cricothyroid ligament forms which structure inside the larynx?

options.text: Vestibular ligament
Median thyrohyoid ligament
Cricotracheal ligament
Vocal ligament

questions.explanation: The free superior edge of the cricothyroid ligament is thickened into the vocal ligament beneath the true vocal fold.

distractorExplanations.A: The vestibular ligament is the thickened inferior edge of the quadrangular membrane.
distractorExplanations.B: This is an anterior midline thickening of the thyrohyoid membrane outside the laryngeal cavity.
distractorExplanations.C: This connects the lower cricoid border with the first tracheal cartilage.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the ligament underlying the true vocal fold.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic ligaments — cricothyroid ligament

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which structure is formed by the thickened free lower margin of the quadrangular membrane?

options.text: Vocal ligament
Median cricothyroid ligament
Hyo-epiglottic ligament
Vestibular ligament

questions.explanation: The inferior free edge of the quadrangular membrane forms the vestibular ligament beneath the vestibular, or false vocal, fold.

distractorExplanations.A: The vocal ligament arises from the superior edge of the cricothyroid ligament below the quadrangular membrane.
distractorExplanations.B: This is the anterior midline thickening between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
distractorExplanations.C: This attaches the epiglottis to the hyoid bone and is not an edge of the quadrangular membrane.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the ligament underlying the false vocal fold.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic ligaments — quadrangular membrane

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: The posterior attachment of a vocal ligament is identified on an arytenoid cartilage. Which projection provides this attachment?

options.text: Muscular process
Apex of the arytenoid
Vocal process
Inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage

questions.explanation: The vocal ligament attaches posteriorly to the anteriorly projecting vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage.

distractorExplanations.A: The muscular process provides attachment for the posterior and lateral crico-arytenoid muscles.
distractorExplanations.B: The apex articulates with the corniculate cartilage, rather than anchoring the vocal ligament.
distractorExplanations.D: This horn articulates with the cricoid and is not the posterior attachment of the vocal ligament.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the vocal and muscular processes of the arytenoid.

source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Laryngeal cartilages — arytenoid processes

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: In an anatomy teaching scenario, an emergency airway passes through the median cricothyroid ligament. Between which two cartilages is this ligament located?

options.text: Hyoid bone above and thyroid cartilage below
Cricoid cartilage above and first tracheal cartilage below
Thyroid cartilage above and cricoid cartilage below
Epiglottis anteriorly and arytenoid cartilage posteriorly

questions.explanation: The median cricothyroid ligament spans the anterior interval between the inferior thyroid region and the arch of the cricoid.

distractorExplanations.A: This interval is crossed by the thyrohyoid membrane, not the median cricothyroid ligament.
distractorExplanations.B: This interval is crossed by the cricotracheal ligament.
distractorExplanations.D: The quadrangular membrane spans this region, not the median cricothyroid ligament.

questions.learningObjective: Locate the median cricothyroid ligament relative to palpable laryngeal cartilages.
