source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic ligaments — median cricothyroid ligament

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: The trachea begins near C6. At which vertebral level does it normally bifurcate into the main bronchi in the mediastinum?

options.text: T4/T5
C2/C3
C6/C7

questions.explanation: Gray’s describes the trachea extending from C6 to its bifurcation at the T4/T5 level.

distractorExplanations.B: This is above the start of the trachea.
distractorExplanations.C: This is near the lower neck, not the normal mediastinal bifurcation.
distractorExplanations.D: This is much lower in the thorax than the tracheal bifurcation.

questions.learningObjective: Locate the tracheal bifurcation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: On an axial section, the tracheal cartilages are C-shaped. Which description of the open part of each ring is correct?

options.text: It faces posteriorly, where the wall is mainly smooth muscle
It faces anteriorly and is completed by bone
It faces laterally and is completed by skeletal muscle
It faces superiorly and is closed by a vocal fold

questions.explanation: The cartilaginous C is open posteriorly; the posterior tracheal wall is composed mainly of smooth muscle.

distractorExplanations.B: The open part faces posteriorly and is not completed by bone.
distractorExplanations.C: Neither the lateral orientation nor skeletal-muscle composition matches the tracheal wall.
distractorExplanations.D: The rings are transverse, and vocal folds belong to the larynx above the trachea.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the posterior orientation and composition of the membranous tracheal wall.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.subtopic: Bronchial tree — main bronchi and aspiration
questions.prompt: A small inhaled foreign body enters a main bronchus. Which anatomical feature helps explain its greater tendency to enter the right side?

options.text: The left main bronchus is wider and more vertical
The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical
The right main bronchus has no cartilaginous support
The right main bronchus opens directly into the pleural cavity

questions.explanation: The right main bronchus has a wider lumen and a more vertical course, favoring entry of inhaled material.

distractorExplanations.A: These features describe the right main bronchus, not the left.
distractorExplanations.C: Bronchi have cartilaginous support; absence of cartilage is characteristic of bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.D: It enters the lung through its root and hilum, not the pleural space.

questions.learningObjective: Explain right-sided foreign-body entry using main-bronchus anatomy.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchial tree — main bronchi and aspiration

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Bronchoscopy reveals a midline ridge separating the entrances to the right and left main bronchi. What is this ridge called?

options.text: Lingula
Hilum
Carina
Pulmonary ligament

questions.explanation: The carina projects at the lower tracheal bifurcation between the origins of the two main bronchi.

distractorExplanations.A: The lingula is a tongue-like part of the left superior pulmonary lobe.
distractorExplanations.B: The hilum is the area on the medial lung surface where root structures enter and leave.
distractorExplanations.D: This is an inferior pleural fold extending from the lung root, not an intratracheal ridge.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the carina at the tracheal bifurcation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: How many lobar (secondary) bronchi normally supply the right and left lungs, respectively?

options.text: Two on the right and three on the left
One on each side
Three on the right and two on the left
Ten on each side

questions.explanation: Each lobar bronchus supplies one lobe: the right lung has three lobes and the left has two.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the usual right and left lobe counts.
distractorExplanations.B: One main bronchus enters each lung, but each divides into lobar bronchi.
distractorExplanations.D: Approximately ten describes bronchopulmonary segments, not lobar bronchi.

questions.learningObjective: Relate the number of lobar bronchi to pulmonary lobes.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A surgeon plans to remove one bronchopulmonary segment while preserving neighboring segments. Which paired structures supply the functional unit being removed?

options.text: A lobar bronchus and the entire main pulmonary artery
A pulmonary vein and a main bronchus
An intercostal artery and a pleural recess
A segmental bronchus and its accompanying pulmonary artery branch

questions.explanation: A bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a tertiary bronchus with an accompanying branch of the pulmonary artery.

distractorExplanations.A: These supply territories larger than a single bronchopulmonary segment.
distractorExplanations.B: A main bronchus supplies a whole lung, while pulmonary veins tend to run between segments.
distractorExplanations.C: These are not the defining airway and arterial supply of a lung segment.

questions.learningObjective: Define a bronchopulmonary segment by its airway and arterial supply.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: During anatomical segmentectomy, which vessels are typically encountered between neighboring bronchopulmonary segments rather than centrally accompanying a segmental bronchus?

options.text: Tributaries of the pulmonary veins
Segmental pulmonary arteries
The pulmonary trunk
Internal thoracic arteries

questions.explanation: Pulmonary venous tributaries tend to run between and around segment margins, whereas segmental bronchi and pulmonary arteries supply the segments.

distractorExplanations.B: These accompany the segmental bronchi into the bronchopulmonary segments.
distractorExplanations.C: The pulmonary trunk is in the mediastinum and divides before the arteries enter the lungs.
distractorExplanations.D: These run along the anterior thoracic wall and do not define intersegmental pulmonary planes.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish intersegmental pulmonary veins from intrasegmental bronchovascular structures.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which two lobes are separated by the horizontal fissure of the right lung?

options.text: Superior and inferior lobes only
Middle and inferior lobes
Superior and inferior lobes of the left lung
Superior and middle lobes

questions.explanation: The right horizontal fissure separates the superior lobe from the middle lobe; the oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from both.

distractorExplanations.A: The oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from the superior and middle lobes.
distractorExplanations.B: These are separated by part of the oblique fissure, not the horizontal fissure.
distractorExplanations.C: The left lung has an oblique fissure but no normal horizontal fissure.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the lobes adjacent to the right horizontal fissure.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Right lung — lobes and fissures

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A tongue-like projection extends from the anterior border of the left lung over the cardiac bulge. To which lobe does it belong?

options.text: Inferior lobe of the left lung
Middle lobe of the left lung
Superior lobe of the left lung
Middle lobe of the right lung

questions.explanation: The lingula projects from the lower part of the left superior lobe; it is not a separate middle lobe.

distractorExplanations.A: The lingula is anterior and belongs to the superior, not the inferior, lobe.
distractorExplanations.B: The normal left lung has no separate middle lobe.
distractorExplanations.D: The described projection is the left lingula, not the right middle lobe.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the lingula as part of the left superior lobe.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A nerve is seen descending immediately anterior to the root of a lung. Which nerve is most consistent with this relationship?

options.text: Vagus nerve
An intercostal nerve
Phrenic nerve
Hypoglossal nerve

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve passes immediately anterior to the lung root; the vagus passes immediately posterior.

distractorExplanations.A: The vagus runs posterior, not anterior, to the lung root.
distractorExplanations.B: Intercostal nerves follow intercostal spaces rather than descending across the front of the lung root.
distractorExplanations.D: XII is a cranial nerve of the tongue and does not descend past the lung root.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish phrenic and vagus nerve relationships to the lung root.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Root and hilum — neighboring nerves

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.subtopic: Root and hilum — right superior lobar bronchus
questions.prompt: Which structure normally lies superior to the pulmonary artery within the root of the right lung?

options.text: Bronchus to the superior lobe
Inferior pulmonary vein
Pulmonary ligament
Left main bronchus

questions.explanation: On the right, the superior lobar bronchus branches within the root and lies above the pulmonary artery.

distractorExplanations.B: Pulmonary veins occupy the inferior part of the root rather than lying above this artery.
distractorExplanations.C: The pulmonary ligament extends inferiorly from the root.
distractorExplanations.D: The left main bronchus is a structure of the left lung root, not the right.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the eparterial position of the right superior lobar bronchus.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Root and hilum — right superior lobar bronchus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.subtopic: Bronchial arteries and veins — nutritive circulation
questions.prompt: Which arterial system supplies the bronchial walls and glands, walls of large pulmonary vessels, and visceral pleura as their nutritive circulation?

options.text: Pulmonary arteries alone
Bronchial arteries
Coronary arteries
Superior epigastric arteries

questions.explanation: Bronchial arteries provide the nutritive vascular supply of these pulmonary tissues and connect with pulmonary vessels within the lung.

distractorExplanations.A: Pulmonary arteries deliver deoxygenated blood for gas exchange; the named nutritive system is the bronchial circulation.
distractorExplanations.C: Coronary arteries supply the heart, not the bronchial walls and visceral pleura.
distractorExplanations.D: These descend into the anterior abdominal wall and are not the pulmonary nutritive vessels.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish bronchial nutritive supply from pulmonary gas-exchange circulation.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchial arteries and veins — nutritive circulation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: In an upright patient, pleural fluid accumulates in the large recess between the inferior lung margin and the inferior pleural reflection. Which recess is this?

options.text: Costodiaphragmatic recess
Costomediastinal recess
Pulmonary hilum
Pericardial cavity

questions.explanation: This recess lies between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, below the inferior lung edge, and is a potential site of fluid collection.

distractorExplanations.B: This lies anteriorly where costal and mediastinal pleura oppose one another, not along the inferior lung margin.
distractorExplanations.C: The hilum is the entry and exit area for root structures, not this inferior pleural recess.
distractorExplanations.D: The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart and is separate from the pleural cavity.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the costodiaphragmatic recess as a site of pleural fluid accumulation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.subtopic: Pleural reflections and inferior lung border
questions.prompt: During quiet respiration, which rib levels approximately mark the inferior lung border and the inferior pleural reflection at the midaxillary line?

options.text: Lung at rib 6; pleura at rib 8
Lung at rib 10; pleura at rib 12
Lung at rib 8; pleura at rib 10
Both at rib 8

questions.explanation: At the midaxillary line the lung reaches approximately rib 8 while the pleural cavity extends to rib 10, leaving a recess below the lung.

distractorExplanations.A: These are the usual midclavicular, not midaxillary, landmarks.
distractorExplanations.B: These values do not describe the midaxillary rib landmarks; posterior limits are described using vertebral levels.
distractorExplanations.D: The pleural reflection extends farther inferiorly than the lung edge and therefore leaves a recess.

questions.learningObjective: Compare lung and pleural lower borders at the midaxillary line.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Pleural reflections and inferior lung border

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Irritation of the mediastinal pleura is felt near the shoulder rather than being sharply localized over the lateral chest wall. Which nerve carries the relevant pleural afferents?

options.text: Phrenic nerve
Intercostal nerves
Vagus nerve
Long thoracic nerve

questions.explanation: Mediastinal pleural afferents travel mainly with the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), accounting for referral toward the neck and supraclavicular shoulder region.

distractorExplanations.B: They supply costal pleura, whose pain is felt in relation to the thoracic wall.
distractorExplanations.C: The vagus contributes to pulmonary visceral innervation, not the somatic afferent supply specified here.
distractorExplanations.D: This nerve supplies serratus anterior and is not the sensory nerve of the mediastinal pleura.

questions.learningObjective: Relate mediastinal pleural sensation to phrenic referred pain.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Parietal pleura — phrenic sensory supply

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which nerves account for localized thoracic-wall pain caused by irritation of the costal pleura?

options.text: Phrenic nerves
Vagus nerves
Recurrent laryngeal nerves
Intercostal nerves

questions.explanation: The costal parietal pleura receives somatic afferents through intercostal nerves, allowing pain to be felt in the corresponding thoracic wall.

distractorExplanations.A: Phrenic nerves mainly supply mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleural sensation, not the costal territory asked about.
distractorExplanations.B: Vagal pulmonary branches are not the somatic sensory supply of costal pleura.
distractorExplanations.C: These supply laryngeal structures and do not supply the costal pleura.

questions.learningObjective: Identify somatic sensory innervation of the costal pleura.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Parietal pleura — costal sensory supply

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Air entering the pleural cavity allows a lung to recoil and collapse. Between which two surfaces has the air accumulated?

options.text: Visceral pleura and parietal pleura
Visceral pleura and the lung surface to which it adheres
Two layers of the pericardium
Tracheal mucosa and tracheal cartilage

questions.explanation: The pleural cavity is the potential space between visceral pleura covering the lung and parietal pleura lining the thoracic boundaries.

distractorExplanations.B: Visceral pleura is firmly attached to the lung; the normal pleural cavity is external to it.
distractorExplanations.C: That is the pericardial cavity, not the pleural space.
distractorExplanations.D: This is within the airway wall and is not the cavity surrounding the lung.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the pleural potential space involved in pneumothorax.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A thin fold of pleura extends inferiorly from the lung root toward the mediastinum. Which structure is being identified?

options.text: Ligamentum arteriosum
Pulmonary ligament
Suprapleural membrane
Oblique fissure

questions.explanation: The pulmonary ligament is the blade-like pleural fold extending inferiorly from the lung root and hilum toward the mediastinum.

distractorExplanations.A: This is a vascular remnant connecting the pulmonary arterial region and aortic arch, not a fold descending from the hilum.
distractorExplanations.C: The suprapleural membrane is fascia over the cervical pleura at the thoracic inlet.
distractorExplanations.D: An oblique fissure separates pulmonary lobes; it is not the pleural fold below the root.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the pulmonary ligament as an inferior pleural fold.

source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Root and hilum — pulmonary ligament

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.chapter: Nasal cavities and relationships to adjacent cavities
questions.prompt: In this anterolateral upper-airway source diagram, which structure is centered at marker A?

options.text: Soft palate
Oral cavity
Nasal septum
Nasopharynx

questions.explanation: Marker A identifies the Nasal septum. The nasal septum is the median wall separating the right and left nasal cavities.

distractorExplanations.A: Soft palate is not the marked target. The soft palate is the movable posterior continuation of the hard palate; it forms the boundary below the nasopharynx.
distractorExplanations.B: Oral cavity is not the marked target. The oral cavity lies inferior to the nasal cavities and anterior to the oropharynx; it is represented by the pink space.
distractorExplanations.D: Nasopharynx is not the marked target. The nasopharynx lies behind the choanae and above the soft palate; it occupies the superior green space.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the Nasal septum and distinguish it from adjacent structures.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: In this coronal nasal-region source diagram, which structure is centered at marker A?

options.text: Inferior nasal concha
Maxillary sinus
Middle nasal concha
Ethmoidal air cells

questions.explanation: Marker A identifies the Maxillary sinus. The maxillary sinus is the large air cavity within the body of the maxilla, lateral to the nasal cavity and inferior to the orbit.

distractorExplanations.A: Inferior nasal concha is not the marked target. The inferior concha is the lowest bony shelf on the lateral nasal wall and is a separate bone.
distractorExplanations.C: Middle nasal concha is not the marked target. The middle concha projects from the ethmoid into the nasal cavity above the inferior concha.
distractorExplanations.D: Ethmoidal air cells is not the marked target. The ethmoidal air cells are small cavities in the ethmoidal labyrinth between the nasal cavity and the orbit.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the Maxillary sinus and distinguish it from adjacent structures.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.chapter: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles and inlet landmarks
questions.prompt: In this posterior laryngeal source diagram, which structure is centered at marker A?

options.text: Cricoid cartilage
Cuneiform tubercle
Corniculate tubercle
Epiglottis

questions.explanation: Marker A identifies the Epiglottis. The epiglottis is the leaf-shaped cartilage forming the anterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet.

distractorExplanations.A: Cricoid cartilage is not the marked target. The broad posterior cricoid lamina supports the posterior crico-arytenoid muscles; its exposed cartilaginous edges are pale blue-gray.
distractorExplanations.B: Cuneiform tubercle is not the marked target. This mucosal prominence overlies a cuneiform cartilage in the aryepiglottic fold, anterior to the corniculate prominence.
distractorExplanations.C: Corniculate tubercle is not the marked target. This prominence overlies a corniculate cartilage at the apex of an arytenoid, posterior to the cuneiform prominence.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the Epiglottis and distinguish it from adjacent structures.

options.text: Pulmonary veins at the right lung root
Bronchus at the right lung root
Pulmonary artery at the right lung root

acceptedFreeText: Bronchus at the right lung root
questions.explanation: Marker A identifies the Bronchus at the right lung root. The cartilaginous airway at the right root is shown with a tan lumen and pale cartilaginous wall. The source labels it generically as bronchus.

distractorExplanations.A: Pulmonary veins at the right lung root is not the marked target. The red vessels leave the right lung carrying oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
distractorExplanations.C: Pulmonary artery at the right lung root is not the marked target. The purple vessel carries deoxygenated blood into the right lung; it is distinct from the pale-ringed bronchus and red pulmonary veins.
distractorExplanations.D: Pulmonary ligament below the right lung root is not the marked target. The inferior blue pleural fold continues down from the right root; it is the pulmonary ligament, not a vessel or bronchus.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the Bronchus at the right lung root and distinguish it from adjacent structures.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A reconstruction of a 4-week embryo shows the earliest respiratory diverticulum. From which site should this bud arise?

options.text: The dorsal wall of the midgut
The surface ectoderm over the future thorax
The ventral wall of the foregut
The somatic mesoderm lining the body wall

questions.explanation: The lung bud appears at approximately 4 weeks as an outgrowth of the ventral foregut wall. Its endoderm gives rise to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract.

distractorExplanations.A: The respiratory diverticulum arises from foregut, not midgut, and from its ventral rather than dorsal wall.
distractorExplanations.B: Surface ectoderm does not form the respiratory diverticulum.
distractorExplanations.D: Somatic mesoderm contributes to the parietal pleura, not the foregut epithelial bud.

questions.learningObjective: Locate the embryonic origin of the respiratory diverticulum.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A lineage-tracing experiment separately labels foregut endoderm and surrounding splanchnic mesoderm. Which pairing correctly predicts the labeled derivatives in the developing lung?

options.text: Endoderm: airway epithelium; splanchnic mesoderm: cartilage and smooth muscle
Endoderm: cartilage; splanchnic mesoderm: airway epithelium
Endoderm: bronchial connective tissue; splanchnic mesoderm: alveolar epithelial lining
Endoderm: airway smooth muscle; splanchnic mesoderm: bronchial epithelial cells

questions.explanation: Respiratory epithelial linings derive from foregut endoderm. Cartilaginous, muscular, and connective-tissue elements of the trachea and lungs derive from surrounding visceral (splanchnic) mesoderm.

distractorExplanations.B: This reverses the epithelial and supporting-tissue lineages.
distractorExplanations.C: Bronchial connective tissue is mesodermal, while the alveolar epithelial lining is endodermal.
distractorExplanations.D: This again reverses the endodermal epithelium and mesodermal smooth muscle.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish endodermal from splanchnic-mesodermal respiratory derivatives.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Which signaling relationship between adjacent tissues normally promotes induction of the respiratory diverticulum?

options.text: Mesodermal retinoic acid upregulates TBX4 in somatic mesoderm
Endodermal retinoic acid upregulates TBX4 in somatic mesoderm
Endodermal retinoic acid upregulates TBX4 in surrounding splanchnic mesoderm
Mesodermal retinoic acid upregulates TBX4 in foregut endoderm

questions.explanation: In the account given in Langman and E1, mesodermal retinoic acid upregulates TBX4 in foregut endoderm. TBX4 promotes lung-bud formation and subsequent pulmonary growth and differentiation.

distractorExplanations.A: The cited TBX4 response occurs in the foregut endoderm at the respiratory-bud site, not in somatic mesoderm.
distractorExplanations.B: This misplaces both the retinoic-acid source and the TBX4-responsive tissue.
distractorExplanations.C: This reverses the described direction: adjacent mesoderm supplies retinoic acid and foregut endoderm expresses the upregulated TBX4.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the retinoic-acid/TBX4 relationship in early lung-bud induction.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Two longitudinal tracheoesophageal ridges fuse during separation of the respiratory primordium from the foregut. Which final arrangement should result?

options.text: Ventral esophagus and dorsal trachea
Dorsal esophagus and ventral trachea
A single foregut lumen still serving both trachea and esophagus
A trachea completely disconnected from the pharynx

questions.explanation: Fusion of the tracheoesophageal ridges forms the septum that separates a dorsal esophageal compartment from a ventral tracheal compartment. The respiratory primordium retains communication with the pharynx through the laryngeal orifice.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the normal dorsal-ventral relationship.
distractorExplanations.C: Successful septation separates the tracheal and esophageal compartments rather than leaving a shared lumen.
distractorExplanations.D: The respiratory primordium normally remains connected to the pharynx through the laryngeal opening.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the orientation and result of tracheoesophageal septation.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: An infant has an upper esophageal segment that ends blindly and a lower esophageal segment communicating with the trachea. Which developmental error best accounts for this arrangement?

options.text: Abnormal partitioning by the tracheoesophageal septum
Failure of laryngeal epithelial recanalization
Abnormal fusion of pleuropericardial folds
Dilation of terminal or larger bronchi

questions.explanation: The arrangement is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula, the most frequent pattern described in Langman. It reflects abnormal partitioning of the foregut into respiratory and esophageal components.

distractorExplanations.B: Laryngeal recanalization reopens the laryngeal lumen; it does not explain the separated upper esophagus and distal tracheal connection.
distractorExplanations.C: Pleuropericardial folds partition body cavities rather than the foregut lumen.
distractorExplanations.D: Bronchial dilation produces congenital lung cysts, not this esophageal-tracheal arrangement.

questions.learningObjective: Connect esophageal atresia with distal fistula to faulty foregut partitioning.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: In a fetus with an obstructed esophageal passage, the volume of amniotic fluid becomes excessive. Which mechanism most directly explains this association?

options.text: An obstructed esophagus directly increases secretion by fetal bronchial glands
Resorption of lung fluid into blood and lymph capillaries is the primary blocked pathway
Swallowed amniotic fluid cannot pass normally into the stomach and intestine
Increased fetal breathing movements are the primary cause of excess amniotic fluid

questions.explanation: Esophageal obstruction can prevent swallowed amniotic fluid from reaching the gastrointestinal tract. This impaired passage accounts for polyhydramnios in relevant tracheoesophageal malformations.

distractorExplanations.A: The source relates the excess fluid to impaired swallowed-fluid passage, not a direct increase in bronchial gland secretion.
distractorExplanations.B: Blood and lymph resorption is important in lung-fluid clearance at birth; it is not the esophageal pathway obstructed here.
distractorExplanations.D: Fetal breathing movements support lung development; the direct association here is loss of normal gastrointestinal passage of swallowed fluid.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why impaired esophageal passage may produce polyhydramnios.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: An infant with a tracheoesophageal fistula also has vertebral, anal, and limb abnormalities. Which additional category belongs to the same VACTERL association?

options.text: Congenital pulmonary cysts
Renal malformations
Ectopic pulmonary lobes
Failure of laryngeal recanalization

questions.explanation: VACTERL includes vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula/esophageal atresia, renal anomalies, and limb defects. It describes a nonrandom association of congenital abnormalities.

distractorExplanations.A: Congenital pulmonary cysts are lung abnormalities but are not one of the defining VACTERL categories.
distractorExplanations.C: Ectopic pulmonary lobes are not one of the named VACTERL categories.
distractorExplanations.D: Laryngeal recanalization defects are not one of the named VACTERL categories.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the congenital anomaly categories of VACTERL.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: The epithelial lining of the developing larynx is endodermal. Its cartilages and muscles are associated with mesenchyme of which pharyngeal arches?

options.text: First and second
Second and third
Third and fifth
Fourth and sixth

questions.explanation: Langman attributes the laryngeal cartilages and muscles to mesenchyme of the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches. This arch origin explains their vagal innervation.

distractorExplanations.A: The first and second arches are not the pair responsible for the laryngeal cartilages and muscles described here.
distractorExplanations.B: The second and third arches are not the specified laryngeal pair.
distractorExplanations.C: The relevant pair is fourth and sixth, not third and fifth.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the pharyngeal arches contributing to laryngeal structures.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A developing laryngeal muscle is derived from the sixth pharyngeal arch. Which nerve is expected to supply it?

options.text: Superior laryngeal branch of the vagus
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus
Facial nerve

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus supplies sixth-arch derivatives. The superior laryngeal branch supplies fourth-arch derivatives.

distractorExplanations.A: The superior laryngeal branch is associated with fourth-arch derivatives.
distractorExplanations.B: The lecture associates the glossopharyngeal nerve with the third arch, not the sixth.
distractorExplanations.D: The lecture associates the facial nerve with the second arch, not the sixth.

questions.learningObjective: Match fourth- and sixth-arch derivatives with their vagal branches.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Rapid epithelial proliferation temporarily closes the developing laryngeal lumen. What normally follows to establish the lateral recesses between the future vocal folds?

options.text: Fusion of the pleuropericardial folds
Vacuolization and recanalization forming the laryngeal ventricles
Formation of a permanent tracheoesophageal fistula
Dilation of tertiary bronchi

questions.explanation: The temporarily occluded laryngeal lumen undergoes vacuolization and recanalization. A pair of lateral laryngeal ventricles develops, bounded by tissue that forms the false and true vocal folds.

distractorExplanations.A: Pleuropericardial folds separate thoracic cavities; they do not reopen the laryngeal lumen.
distractorExplanations.C: A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal connection and is not part of normal laryngeal recanalization.
distractorExplanations.D: Tertiary bronchial development occurs in the branching lungs, not in the laryngeal ventricles.

questions.learningObjective: Describe recanalization of the larynx and formation of its ventricles.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A developmental model is being labeled at the secondary bronchial stage. Which branching pattern correctly predicts the normal lung lobes?

options.text: Two right secondary bronchi and three left secondary bronchi
One secondary bronchus on each side
Ten right secondary bronchi and eight left secondary bronchi
Three right secondary bronchi and two left secondary bronchi

questions.explanation: The right primary bronchus gives rise to three secondary bronchi and the left to two, corresponding to three right lung lobes and two left lobes.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the normal right-left lobar pattern.
distractorExplanations.B: One primary bronchus supplies each lung, but each subdivides into multiple secondary bronchi.
distractorExplanations.C: The ten-right/eight-left count in Langman refers to tertiary segmental bronchi, not secondary lobar bronchi.

questions.learningObjective: Relate secondary bronchial branching to pulmonary lobes.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: During repeated branching of the secondary bronchi, tertiary bronchi establish the units later called bronchopulmonary segments. What level of the bronchial tree is represented by a tertiary bronchus?

options.text: A segmental bronchus
A primary bronchus supplying an entire lung
A lobar bronchus
An alveolar duct

questions.explanation: Tertiary bronchi are segmental bronchi. Their branching territories establish the bronchopulmonary segments, whereas secondary bronchi are lobar.

distractorExplanations.B: Primary bronchi are the right and left main bronchi, one for each lung.
distractorExplanations.C: Lobar bronchi are secondary rather than tertiary branches.
distractorExplanations.D: Alveolar ducts are much more distal gas-exchange passages, not tertiary bronchi.

questions.learningObjective: Relate primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchial levels to lungs, lobes, and segments.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: In a developing-lung explant, the bronchial epithelium is intact but signaling from surrounding mesoderm is disrupted. Which process is most directly threatened by loss of mesodermal fibroblast-growth-factor signals?

options.text: Recanalization of the temporarily occluded laryngeal lumen
Branching morphogenesis of the bronchial tree
Partitioning of the foregut by tracheoesophageal ridges
Clearance of fetal lung fluid at the first breath

questions.explanation: Bronchial branching depends on epithelial-mesenchymal interactions between lung-bud endoderm and surrounding visceral mesoderm. Members of the FGF family are among the mesodermal branching signals.

distractorExplanations.A: The cited epithelial-mesenchymal FGF signal concerns lung branching rather than the separate process of laryngeal recanalization.
distractorExplanations.C: Foregut septation is a distinct earlier morphogenetic event, not the branching interaction specified in this experiment.
distractorExplanations.D: Lung-fluid clearance occurs during the transition at birth and is not the bronchial-branching role described for these signals.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of epithelial-mesenchymal signaling in bronchial branching.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A lineage map distinguishes the membrane covering the developing lung from the membrane lining the inner thoracic wall. Which origin pairing is correct?

options.text: Visceral pleura from endoderm; parietal pleura from splanchnic mesoderm
Both layers from foregut endoderm
Visceral pleura from somatic mesoderm; parietal pleura from splanchnic mesoderm
Visceral pleura from splanchnic mesoderm; parietal pleura from somatic mesoderm

questions.explanation: The mesoderm covering the lung becomes visceral pleura. The somatic mesoderm lining the body wall becomes parietal pleura. The space between the two is the pleural cavity.

distractorExplanations.A: Endoderm supplies respiratory epithelial linings, not visceral pleural mesothelium.
distractorExplanations.B: The pleural layers are mesodermal, not foregut-endodermal.
distractorExplanations.C: This reverses the visceral and somatic mesoderm relationships.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the embryonic origins of visceral and parietal pleura.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: The expanding lungs occupy pericardioperitoneal canals. Which structures close the communication of these future pleural spaces with the peritoneal cavity?

options.text: Pleuroperitoneal folds or membranes
Tracheoesophageal ridges
Pleuropericardial folds alone
Laryngeal ventricles

questions.explanation: Pleuroperitoneal folds separate the canals from the peritoneal cavity. Pleuropericardial folds separately divide them from the pericardial cavity.

distractorExplanations.B: Tracheoesophageal ridges separate the respiratory and esophageal portions of the foregut.
distractorExplanations.C: Pleuropericardial folds separate pleural from pericardial spaces; the question asks about the peritoneal connection.
distractorExplanations.D: Laryngeal ventricles are recesses within the larynx, not partitions between body cavities.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate pleuroperitoneal from pleuropericardial separation.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A fetal lung at 12 weeks has a branching tree ending in terminal bronchioles. Which finding is expected at this developmental stage?

options.text: Terminal sacs closely apposed to capillaries throughout the lung
Mature alveoli with fully developed epithelial-endothelial contacts
No respiratory bronchioles or alveoli yet
Respiratory bronchioles already dividing into alveolar ducts

questions.explanation: Twelve weeks falls within the pseudoglandular period listed as 5-16 weeks in Langman. Branching has formed terminal bronchioles, but respiratory bronchioles and alveoli are not yet present.

distractorExplanations.A: Terminal-sac formation with close capillary contact characterizes a later maturation period.
distractorExplanations.B: Well-developed alveolar epithelial-endothelial contacts are a later maturation feature.
distractorExplanations.D: Respiratory bronchiolar and alveolar-duct differentiation is a canalicular-period feature, later than this pseudoglandular specimen.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the structural limit of the pseudoglandular period.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A 20-week fetal lung shows terminal bronchioles dividing into respiratory bronchioles, with further branches toward alveolar ducts and increasing vascularity. Which developmental period best fits?

options.text: Pseudoglandular period
Postnatal alveolar period
Initial fourth-week lung-bud period
Canalicular period

questions.explanation: The canalicular period is listed as 16-26 weeks. Terminal bronchioles form respiratory bronchioles, which branch into alveolar ducts, while vascular development increases.

distractorExplanations.A: The earlier pseudoglandular period lacks respiratory bronchioles and alveoli.
distractorExplanations.B: The specimen is prenatal and at 20 weeks, not in postnatal alveolar multiplication.
distractorExplanations.C: The fourth-week stage concerns initial foregut budding, long before this distal branching pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the canalicular period from age and distal airway differentiation.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: During late fetal lung development, terminal sacs form and the epithelium becomes much thinner as capillaries approach it. What functional improvement follows most directly?

options.text: More efficient mucus propulsion from newly formed alveolar cilia
Increased filtration by a thicker alveolar epithelial layer
A shorter diffusion distance across the developing blood-air barrier
Greater stability from a new cartilage layer around each terminal sac

questions.explanation: Flattening of type I alveolar epithelial cells and their close contact with capillaries create a thin blood-air barrier. This structural maturation supports increasingly effective gas exchange.

distractorExplanations.A: The developing gas-exchange lining becomes thin type I epithelium, not a ciliated mucus-transport surface.
distractorExplanations.B: The epithelium becomes thinner, not thicker, thereby reducing the gas diffusion distance.
distractorExplanations.D: Terminal sacs develop close epithelial-capillary contacts, not a cartilage-supported wall.

questions.learningObjective: Connect terminal-sac epithelial thinning and capillary apposition to gas-exchange capability.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Near the end of 24 weeks, a fetal alveolar epithelial population begins producing a phospholipid-rich secretion that lowers surface tension. Which population is responsible?

options.text: Type I alveolar epithelial cells
Type II alveolar epithelial cells
Pleural mesothelial cells
Pulmonary capillary endothelial cells

questions.explanation: Langman describes the development of type II alveolar epithelial cells at the end of 24 weeks. Their surfactant reduces surface tension at the air-alveolar interface; production increases as the lung matures.

distractorExplanations.A: Type I cells become thin elements of the diffusion barrier rather than the principal surfactant-secreting population.
distractorExplanations.C: Pleural mesothelium forms the serosal covering of the lungs, not the alveolar surfactant-producing cells.
distractorExplanations.D: Endothelium forms the vascular side of the blood-air barrier, not the epithelial surfactant source.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the fetal cell population responsible for surfactant production.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A premature newborn has insufficient pulmonary surfactant. Which mechanical sequence most directly explains the resulting respiratory distress?

options.text: Higher air-liquid surface tension followed by alveolar collapse during expiration
Lower air-liquid surface tension followed by excessive alveolar expansion
A primary increase in epithelial thickness that mechanically seals the alveolar lumen
A primary contraction of bronchiolar smooth muscle that closes otherwise stable alveoli

questions.explanation: Without sufficient surfactant, surface tension remains high at the alveolar air-liquid interface. Primitive alveoli are therefore more prone to collapse during expiration, contributing to neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

distractorExplanations.B: Surfactant deficiency raises surface tension and favors collapse, not excessive expansion.
distractorExplanations.C: The direct mechanical consequence of deficient surfactant is increased surface tension rather than epithelial thickening that seals the lumen.
distractorExplanations.D: The key abnormality in surfactant-deficiency respiratory distress is alveolar instability, not primary bronchiolar muscle constriction.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the surface-tension mechanism of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: At the onset of breathing, fetal lung fluid must be cleared while the alveolar surface remains protected against collapse. Which statement best describes the normal transition?

options.text: All surfactant is expelled with the fluid before the first breath
Most fluid is expelled through the trachea and bronchi, with little capillary resorption
Most fluid is resorbed into blood and lymph capillaries while surfactant remains as a surface coat
Most fluid passes directly from the lungs into the esophagus while the capillaries remain uninvolved

questions.explanation: Most fetal lung fluid is rapidly resorbed by blood and lymph capillaries when breathing begins. Surfactant remains on alveolar cell surfaces as a thin phospholipid coat, lowering surface tension as air enters.

distractorExplanations.A: Retaining the surfactant coat is important for alveolar stability; it is not all expelled before breathing.
distractorExplanations.B: The source allows a small amount of fluid to be expelled through the airways, but identifies blood and lymph capillary resorption as the main route.
distractorExplanations.D: The normal main pathway is capillary resorption; there is no direct lung-to-esophagus conduit for most fluid.

questions.learningObjective: Describe fetal lung-fluid clearance and surfactant retention at birth.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: Before birth, the fetus makes respiratory movements that draw amniotic fluid into the airways. What is the developmental importance of these movements?

options.text: They stimulate lung development and condition respiratory muscles
They keep the fetal lungs free of fluid before birth
They substitute for surfactant in stabilizing air-filled fetal alveoli
They deliver the main supply of surfactant from the amniotic cavity into the lungs

questions.explanation: Fetal breathing movements begin before birth and are important for lung growth and conditioning of respiratory muscles. They occur in fluid-filled lungs and are not the start of atmospheric air breathing.

distractorExplanations.B: Fetal lungs remain fluid-filled; these movements draw in amniotic fluid rather than keeping them dry.
distractorExplanations.C: The fetal lungs are not air-filled, and surfactant remains essential for stable ventilation after birth.
distractorExplanations.D: Type II cells in the fetal lung produce surfactant; breathing movements are not its principal external delivery system.

questions.learningObjective: State the developmental roles of fetal breathing movements.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A comparison of newborn and childhood lungs shows a major increase in gas-exchange capacity. Which process accounts for most postnatal lung growth described in Langman?

options.text: Enlargement of the original alveoli without formation of new ones
Enlargement of pleural spaces without additional gas-exchange surface
Dilation of existing bronchi without addition of distal respiratory units
Increase in the number of respiratory bronchioles and alveoli

questions.explanation: Postnatal lung growth is primarily due to formation of additional respiratory bronchioles and alveoli, rather than simply enlargement of the alveoli present at birth. Langman describes continued alveolar formation during the first 10 years.

distractorExplanations.A: Alveoli increase somewhat in size, but this is not the principal growth mechanism described.
distractorExplanations.B: Expansion of pleural space without more respiratory tissue would not explain the growth in gas-exchange capacity.
distractorExplanations.C: Conducting bronchial dilation alone does not account for the increase in distal respiratory units described in postnatal growth.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish postnatal alveolar multiplication from enlargement alone.

questions.subject: embryology
questions.prompt: A child has multiple congenital cystic spaces in the lung that drain poorly and develop recurrent infections. Which developmental alteration best matches the congenital lung cysts described in the source?

options.text: Formation of independent additional respiratory buds from the foregut
Dilation of terminal or larger bronchi
Faulty separation of the trachea and esophagus
Insufficient differentiation of surfactant-producing epithelial cells

questions.explanation: Langman describes congenital lung cysts as dilations of terminal or larger bronchi. Their poor drainage predisposes to chronic infection; they may be multiple or occur as one or more larger cysts.

distractorExplanations.A: Independent additional respiratory buds are the proposed origin of ectopic pulmonary lobes, not the bronchial cysts described here.
distractorExplanations.C: Faulty tracheoesophageal separation produces atresia or fistula rather than these intrapulmonary cystic spaces.
distractorExplanations.D: Insufficient surfactant-producing cell maturation causes neonatal alveolar instability and respiratory distress, not congenital bronchial cysts.

questions.learningObjective: Connect congenital pulmonary cysts with bronchial dilation and poor drainage.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Serial sections follow an airway distally from a terminal bronchiole. Which new finding first establishes that the airway has entered the respiratory portion of the lung?

options.text: A continuous layer of ciliated columnar cells
Alveoli opening directly from the airway wall
Seromucous glands beneath the epithelium
Irregular plates of hyaline cartilage

questions.explanation: Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways with alveoli opening from their walls. These openings permit gas exchange; terminal bronchioles remain entirely conducting airways.

distractorExplanations.A: Ciliated epithelium also occurs in conducting airways and does not establish a gas-exchange region.
distractorExplanations.C: Seromucous glands characterize more proximal conducting airways and are absent from bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.D: Cartilage supports bronchi; it is absent from bronchioles and the alveolar region.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the terminal conducting airway from the first respiratory airway.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A specimen from an inferior nasal concha has a vascular lamina propria and small seromucous glands. Which pairing best explains how this mucosa conditions inspired air?

options.text: Cartilage warms the air; cilia supply water
Goblet cells warm the air; bone removes particles
Basal cells humidify the air; capillaries produce mucus
Superficial blood vessels warm the air; glandular water humidifies it

questions.explanation: The rich superficial vascular network transfers heat to inspired air. Water in glandular secretions humidifies it, while mucus traps particles for clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: Cartilage provides support, and cilia move the mucus layer rather than supply water.
distractorExplanations.B: Goblet cells secrete mucin; warming depends chiefly on the underlying vasculature.
distractorExplanations.C: Basal cells are progenitors, and capillaries do not secrete mucus.

questions.learningObjective: Relate the vascular and glandular components of nasal mucosa to air conditioning.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: After a limited toxic injury to the olfactory mucosa, a patient gradually recovers some sense of smell. Which local cell population provides the most direct source of replacement olfactory neurons?

options.text: Basal epithelial stem cells
Mature ciliated respiratory cells
Serous cells of Bowman glands
Alveolar macrophages

questions.explanation: Basal cells in the olfactory epithelium act as stem cells for olfactory neurons and supporting cells. This regenerative capacity can allow recovery after injury confined to the mucosa.

distractorExplanations.B: Mature ciliated respiratory cells clear mucus and are not the olfactory neuronal stem-cell population.
distractorExplanations.C: Bowman gland cells supply serous fluid around olfactory cilia rather than replacement neurons.
distractorExplanations.D: Alveolar macrophages are pulmonary phagocytes, not progenitors in the nasal epithelium.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the regenerative cell population of olfactory epithelium.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: An uncommon columnar cell in respiratory epithelium has a tuft of short apical microvilli and synaptic contact with an afferent nerve ending at its base. What is its principal role?

options.text: Mucin secretion
Replacement of other epithelial cells
Chemosensory reception
Propulsion of the mucus sheet

questions.explanation: This is the description of a brush cell. Its apical microvilli and basal afferent contact support a chemosensory role.

distractorExplanations.A: Mucin secretion is principally a goblet-cell function in this epithelium.
distractorExplanations.B: Basal stem and progenitor cells replace the epithelial populations.
distractorExplanations.D: Mucus propulsion depends on the motile cilia of ciliated columnar cells, not brush-cell microvilli.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate brush-cell function from goblet, basal, and ciliated-cell functions.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A bronchial neoplasm shows neuroendocrine differentiation. Which normal respiratory epithelial population contains dense-core granules and provides the relevant normal counterpart?

options.text: Goblet cells
Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells
Basal stem cells
Ciliated columnar cells

questions.explanation: Small granule or Kulchitsky cells belong to the diffuse neuroendocrine system and contain dense-core granules. Junqueira relates small cell carcinoma to this bronchial epithelial population.

distractorExplanations.A: Goblet cells contain mucin secretory granules and are not the described neuroendocrine population.
distractorExplanations.C: Basal cells are mitotically active progenitors rather than the dense-core-granule endocrine cells.
distractorExplanations.D: Ciliated cells specialize in mucus transport and do not define the neuroendocrine cell population.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the neuroendocrine component of respiratory epithelium.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A bronchial biopsy from a long-term smoker shows replacement of the normal ciliated lining by stratified squamous epithelium. Which protective function is most directly lost in the affected area?

options.text: Elastic recoil of the interalveolar septa
Production of alveolar surfactant by type II cells
Phagocytosis within alveolar air spaces
Ciliary transport of particle-laden mucus

questions.explanation: Squamous metaplasia replaces the ciliated respiratory epithelium with a nonciliated stratified lining. The affected surface can no longer perform normal mucociliary clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: Elastic recoil is a function of elastic fibers in pulmonary tissue, not of the bronchial epithelial cilia.
distractorExplanations.B: Type II pneumocytes are alveolar cells; this biopsy describes a bronchial epithelial change.
distractorExplanations.C: Alveolar macrophages perform phagocytosis independently of the bronchial ciliated lining.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the functional consequence of squamous metaplasia of respiratory epithelium.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A laryngeal flap that deflects swallowed material away from the airway is sampled. Its lingual surface is covered by stratified squamous epithelium. Which tissue normally supports the core of this structure?

options.text: Hyaline cartilage only
A vocal ligament of elastic connective tissue without cartilage
Elastic cartilage
A circular layer of smooth muscle without cartilage

questions.explanation: The structure is the epiglottis. It contains elastic cartilage; its lingual surface has stratified squamous epithelium, with a variable transition to respiratory epithelium on the laryngeal surface.

distractorExplanations.A: Hyaline cartilage supports larger laryngeal elements such as the thyroid and cricoid, not the epiglottic core.
distractorExplanations.B: The vocal ligament supports the free edge of a true vocal fold, not the epiglottic flap.
distractorExplanations.D: Smooth muscle is important in tracheal and bronchial walls but is not the supporting core of the epiglottis.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the epithelial and cartilaginous organization of the epiglottis.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: During phonation, a paired mucosal fold vibrates over an elastic ligament and a striated vocalis muscle. Which epithelium is best suited to the exposed vibrating surface?

options.text: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Simple squamous mesothelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium dominated by club cells
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium

questions.explanation: True vocal folds are covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which protects against abrasion and drying during rapid air movement. The elastic ligament and skeletal vocalis muscle support phonation.

distractorExplanations.B: Mesothelium lines pleural serosal surfaces, not the vibrating surface of a vocal fold.
distractorExplanations.C: Club-cell-rich cuboidal epithelium characterizes terminal bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.D: Respiratory epithelium covers much of the larynx, including much of the vestibular folds, but the exposed true vocal folds have a protective squamous lining.

questions.learningObjective: Relate true vocal-fold epithelium to mechanical stress during phonation.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: During a forceful cough, the posterior muscular bridge between the open ends of tracheal cartilage rings contracts. What is the immediate mechanical effect?

options.text: The tracheal lumen widens and expelled-air velocity falls
The open cartilage ends separate, increasing tracheal diameter
The tracheal diameter remains fixed because the cartilage prevents all narrowing
The tracheal lumen narrows and expelled-air velocity increases

questions.explanation: The trachealis is smooth muscle spanning the posterior gap of the C-shaped cartilage rings. Its contraction narrows the airway during coughing, increasing the velocity of expelled air and aiding clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the cough response; relaxation, rather than contraction, permits widening.
distractorExplanations.B: Contraction of the posterior muscular bridge narrows rather than widens the tracheal lumen.
distractorExplanations.C: The posterior gap in the C-shaped rings permits the trachealis to alter the lumen; the support is not a rigid complete cylinder.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how trachealis contraction contributes to the cough reflex.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A small intrapulmonary airway has a folded epithelial lining and a relatively prominent smooth-muscle wall. Which additional finding most strongly supports classification as a bronchiole rather than a bronchus?

options.text: Seromucous glands and a complete cartilage ring
Absence of both cartilage and mucosal glands
Numerous cartilage plates with occasional lymphoid nodules
A thick squamous lining over a vocal ligament

questions.explanation: Bronchioles lack cartilage and mucosal glands, while retaining smooth muscle. Bronchi have cartilage and glands, although both become less prominent as the branches become smaller.

distractorExplanations.A: Glands and cartilage support a more proximal conducting airway, not a bronchiole.
distractorExplanations.C: Cartilage plates are characteristic of intrapulmonary bronchi.
distractorExplanations.D: A squamous lining over a vocal ligament describes a true vocal fold, not an intrapulmonary airway.

questions.learningObjective: Use cartilage and gland distribution to distinguish bronchioles from bronchi.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A nonciliated, dome-shaped epithelial cell in a terminal bronchiole metabolizes inhaled xenobiotics. Which intracellular compartment is especially important for this activity?

options.text: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum with detoxifying enzymes
Lamellar bodies containing newly stored alveolar surfactant
Motile ciliary axonemes
Apical mucin granules of a goblet cell

questions.explanation: Club cells have smooth endoplasmic reticulum containing detoxifying enzymes, including a P450 system. Their other functions include secretion of protective proteins and surfactant components.

distractorExplanations.B: Lamellar bodies are the characteristic surfactant-storage organelles of type II alveolar cells, not the principal club-cell detoxification compartment.
distractorExplanations.C: Club cells are nonciliated; cilia mediate surface transport rather than xenobiotic metabolism.
distractorExplanations.D: Goblet-cell granules store mucin; they do not provide the described detoxifying enzyme system.

questions.learningObjective: Connect club-cell ultrastructure with xenobiotic detoxification.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: An asthma attack produces abrupt narrowing of small conducting airways. Which histological feature allows these airways to change caliber markedly despite having no cartilage?

options.text: A thick keratinized epithelial layer
An encircling ring of skeletal muscle
A proportionately prominent smooth-muscle layer
A wall made only of fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae

questions.explanation: Bronchioles have a proportionately prominent smooth-muscle layer. Contraction of this layer produces bronchospasm and can sharply reduce the lumen.

distractorExplanations.A: Bronchiolar epithelium is not keratinized, and epithelial keratin does not produce acute constriction.
distractorExplanations.B: Bronchiolar muscle is smooth, not skeletal.
distractorExplanations.D: Fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae characterize the alveolar gas-exchange barrier, not the entire bronchiolar wall.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the structural basis of bronchiolar bronchospasm.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: After a quiet inspiration, the lungs recoil as the inspiratory muscles relax. Which component of the interalveolar septa contributes most directly to this passive recoil?

options.text: Hyaline cartilage plates
Goblet-cell mucin
Reticular fibers resisting excessive distention
Elastic fibers returning toward their unstretched state

questions.explanation: Elastic fibers are stretched during lung expansion and recoil during expiration. Reticular fibers provide a supporting framework and help limit excessive distention, but are not contractile cells.

distractorExplanations.A: Cartilage supports conducting bronchi and is absent from the interalveolar septa.
distractorExplanations.B: Mucin traps material in conducting airways; it is not the recoil element of alveolar walls.
distractorExplanations.C: Reticular fibers do resist excessive distention, but the passive recoil described is most directly associated with elastic fibers.

questions.learningObjective: Differentiate elastic recoil from the supporting role of reticular fibers.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A bronchiole becomes obstructed, yet some air can reach adjacent alveoli through openings in their shared septa. Which structures provide this route?

options.text: Alveolar pores of Kohn
Fenestrations in pulmonary capillary endothelium
Ducts of seromucous glands
Spaces between unsealed type I cells

questions.explanation: Alveolar pores connect neighboring alveoli and allow pressure equilibration and collateral passage of air when a local airway is blocked.

distractorExplanations.B: Pulmonary capillary endothelium is continuous, not fenestrated, and the vascular lumen is not an air passage.
distractorExplanations.C: Seromucous gland ducts open into conducting airways; they do not connect neighboring alveoli.
distractorExplanations.D: Type I cells form tight junctions. Unsealed gaps would disrupt the barrier rather than provide the normal collateral route.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the function of alveolar pores in collateral ventilation.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: At the thinnest part of an interalveolar septum, oxygen crosses from the alveolar lining toward capillary blood. Which sequence correctly lists the principal tissue components encountered?

options.text: Type II cell, cartilage matrix, fenestrated endothelium
Alveolar macrophage, separate thick connective-tissue layers, endothelium
Type I cell cytoplasm, fused basal laminae, capillary endothelial cytoplasm
Ciliated bronchiolar cell, smooth muscle, pulmonary venous wall

questions.explanation: The thin blood-air barrier consists of attenuated type I alveolar epithelium, fused epithelial and capillary basal laminae, and attenuated continuous capillary endothelium. The surfactant film lies on the air-facing surface.

distractorExplanations.A: Type II cells are bulky surfactant-producing cells, cartilage is absent here, and alveolar capillaries are not fenestrated.
distractorExplanations.B: Macrophages are not a continuous lining layer, and a thick connective-tissue interval would impede diffusion.
distractorExplanations.D: This combines conducting-airway and larger-vessel structures rather than the alveolar capillary barrier.

questions.learningObjective: State the tissue components of the thin blood-air barrier.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A student argues that pulmonary capillaries must be fenestrated because gas exchange is rapid. Which ultrastructural description corrects this claim?

options.text: Discontinuous endothelial cells separated by large gaps
Continuous, extremely thin endothelial cells with organelles concentrated near the nucleus
A double layer of cuboidal endothelial cells
An endothelial lining replaced by type II pneumocytes

questions.explanation: Alveolar capillary endothelium is continuous and nonfenestrated. Its attenuated cytoplasm, with most organelles near the nucleus, minimizes the diffusion distance without requiring endothelial pores.

distractorExplanations.A: Large discontinuities are not a normal feature of the alveolar capillary barrier.
distractorExplanations.C: A multilayered cuboidal lining would greatly increase the diffusion distance and is not the normal capillary structure.
distractorExplanations.D: Pneumocytes line the alveolar air side; endothelial cells continue to line the capillary blood side.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that alveolar capillaries are continuous rather than fenestrated.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Morphometry shows that one epithelial population covers about 95% of the alveolar surface despite having very little cytoplasm away from its nucleus. Which population is being measured?

options.text: Alveolar macrophages
Type II pneumocytes
Club cells
Type I pneumocytes

questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes are highly attenuated squamous cells covering approximately 95% of the alveolar lining surface. This percentage refers to surface coverage, not to the proportion of all lung cells.

distractorExplanations.A: Macrophages can lie on alveolar surfaces or in septa but do not form the continuous epithelial lining.
distractorExplanations.B: Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal and cover the smaller remaining portion of the alveolar surface.
distractorExplanations.C: Club cells are characteristic of bronchiolar epithelium, not the broad gas-exchange lining.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish type I surface coverage from type II secretory specialization.

source.title: Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A distal lung passage is lined almost entirely by alveolar openings. Small eosinophilic knobs project between adjacent openings. What do these knobs principally represent?

options.text: Hyaline cartilage islands
Smooth muscle around alveolar openings
Seromucous gland acini
Clusters of type II alveolar cells

questions.explanation: Alveolar ducts are bordered by alveolar openings with strands of smooth muscle around their rims. In sections, this muscle can appear as eosinophilic knobs between alveoli.

distractorExplanations.A: Cartilage is absent from alveolar ducts.
distractorExplanations.C: Mucosal glands are absent from the bronchiolar and alveolar portions of the airway.
distractorExplanations.D: Type II cells are cuboidal epithelial cells within the alveolar lining; the rim-like eosinophilic knobs described here represent smooth muscle.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A pulmonary surfactant preparation contains dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine but lacks proteins needed for its proper orientation within the surface film. Which protein pair is most directly missing?

options.text: SP-A and SP-D
Collagen and elastin
SP-B and SP-C
Mucin and lysozyme

questions.explanation: The hydrophobic proteins SP-B and SP-C are required for the proper organization of DPPC in the alveolar surfactant film. SP-A and SP-D have important innate immune functions.

distractorExplanations.A: SP-A and SP-D are the hydrophilic surfactant proteins emphasized for innate immune protection, not the specified DPPC-orienting pair.

distractorExplanations.D: Mucin and lysozyme contribute to airway defense but are not the SP-B/SP-C pair organizing DPPC.

options.text: SP-A and SP-D
SP-B and SP-C
SP-A and SP-B
SP-C and SP-D

questions.explanation: SP-A and SP-D are hydrophilic surfactant proteins with important innate immune functions. The hydrophobic SP-B and SP-C proteins primarily support the organization of the lipid film.

distractorExplanations.B: SP-B and SP-C are emphasized for proper lipid-film organization, not the immune role asked here.
distractorExplanations.C: SP-A has the immune role, but SP-B is a hydrophobic protein involved in proper lipid-film organization.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Following a limited inhalational injury, many type I alveolar cells are lost. Which surviving epithelial population proliferates and produces progeny capable of restoring both type I and type II cells?

options.text: Ciliated tracheal cells
Alveolar macrophages
Type II pneumocytes
Capillary endothelial cells

questions.explanation: Remaining type II pneumocytes can enter mitosis after alveolar injury. Their progeny provide precursors for both major alveolar epithelial cell types.

distractorExplanations.A: Ciliated tracheal cells belong to a different epithelial compartment and are not the local alveolar progenitor population.
distractorExplanations.B: Macrophages remove debris but do not normally regenerate the pneumocyte lining.
distractorExplanations.D: Endothelial cells repair the vascular lining, not the type I/type II alveolar epithelium.

questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Sputum from a patient with pulmonary congestion contains large phagocytic cells with iron-positive brown pigment. Which description best explains these cells?

options.text: Type II pneumocytes storing DPPC in lamellar bodies
Ciliated cells containing retained mucus
Type I pneumocytes accumulating elastic fibers
Alveolar macrophages containing hemosiderin from ingested erythrocytes

questions.explanation: Alveolar macrophages ingest erythrocytes that escape congested or damaged pulmonary capillaries. Hemosiderin accumulation produces iron-positive heart failure cells, which may reach sputum via airway clearance.

distractorExplanations.A: Lamellar bodies contain surfactant components; they do not explain iron-positive pigment from erythrocyte degradation.
distractorExplanations.B: Ciliated cells move mucus but are not the described large iron-laden phagocytes.
distractorExplanations.C: Type I cells are attenuated epithelial cells, not the principal erythrocyte-clearing phagocytes.

questions.prompt: A vessel follows the bronchial tree, carries oxygen-poor blood, and supplies the dense capillary networks around alveoli. Which vessel best matches this description?

A pulmonary arterial branch
A bronchial arterial branch
A deep pulmonary lymphatic vessel

questions.explanation: Pulmonary arterial branches accompany the bronchial tree and supply the dense capillary networks around alveoli. Pulmonary venules initially course separately through the parenchyma.

distractorExplanations.A: Pulmonary venules collect blood from alveolar capillaries and initially course separately from airways.
distractorExplanations.C: Bronchial arteries also accompany airways, but they carry oxygen-rich systemic blood and chiefly nourish tissues down to respiratory bronchioles.

Parietal pleura lined by simple squamous mesothelium
An interalveolar septum lined by pneumocytes
A small bronchial wall lined by respiratory epithelium

questions.explanation: The visceral pleura covers the lung surface and consists of simple squamous mesothelium over thin connective tissue. It is continuous with parietal pleura at the hilum; a lubricating serous film facilitates movement between them.

distractorExplanations.B: The histological lining is similar, but parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall rather than the outer lung surface.

Simple squamous epithelium

Epiglottic folds built around elastic cartilage
Tracheal folds supported by C-shaped cartilage rings

Odorant receptor-bearing sensory cilia

Type II pneumocyte packaging pulmonary surfactant
Alveolar macrophage digesting phagocytosed debris
Capillary endothelial cell forming the vascular side of the diffusion barrier

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: During quiet inspiration in a healthy adult, which action is the principal cause of the increase in thoracic volume?

options.text: Contraction of the abdominal rectus muscles
Contraction and downward movement of the diaphragm
Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles
Passive recoil of the lungs

questions.explanation: Diaphragmatic contraction pulls the lower surfaces of the lungs downward and is the main driver of normal quiet inspiration.

distractorExplanations.A: Abdominal contraction pushes the diaphragm upward during forceful expiration.
distractorExplanations.C: Internal intercostal contraction helps lower the rib cage during expiration.
distractorExplanations.D: Passive elastic recoil primarily produces quiet expiration, not inspiration.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the principal muscle action responsible for quiet inspiration.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A healthy adult begins a quiet inspiration with an open glottis. Pressures are measured relative to atmospheric pressure. Which combination is expected while air is flowing into the lungs?

options.text: Positive alveolar pressure and less negative pleural pressure
Positive alveolar pressure and more negative pleural pressure
Negative alveolar pressure and positive pleural pressure
Slightly negative alveolar pressure and more negative pleural pressure

questions.explanation: Inspiratory expansion makes pleural pressure more negative and lowers alveolar pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure. The alveolar-to-atmospheric pressure difference drives inward airflow.

distractorExplanations.A: Positive alveolar pressure would drive air outward; pleural pressure normally becomes more negative during inspiration.
distractorExplanations.B: More negative pleural pressure is appropriate, but positive alveolar pressure would oppose inward airflow.
distractorExplanations.C: Quiet inspiration does not make pleural pressure positive; it becomes more negative.

questions.learningObjective: Relate inspiratory airflow to alveolar and pleural pressure changes.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: At one instant during inspiration, alveolar pressure is -1 cm H2O and pleural pressure is -7 cm H2O, both relative to atmosphere. What is the transpulmonary pressure?

options.text: +6 cm H2O
-6 cm H2O
+8 cm H2O
-8 cm H2O

questions.explanation: Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar pressure minus pleural pressure: -1 - (-7) = +6 cm H2O. It is the distending pressure across the lung.

distractorExplanations.B: This reverses the subtraction and gives pleural minus alveolar pressure.
distractorExplanations.C: Adding the absolute values ignores the signed pressure difference.
distractorExplanations.D: Adding the two signed pressures does not calculate transpulmonary pressure.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate transpulmonary pressure using signed pressure measurements.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: After sufficient time for equilibration, increasing transpulmonary pressure from 5 to 7 cm H2O increases the volume of both lungs by 400 mL. What is their compliance over this interval?

options.text: 100 mL/cm H2O
400 mL/cm H2O
200 mL/cm H2O
800 mL/cm H2O

questions.explanation: Compliance equals change in lung volume divided by change in transpulmonary pressure. Here, 400 mL / (7 - 5) cm H2O = 200 mL/cm H2O.

distractorExplanations.A: A value of 100 would require a 4 cm H2O pressure change for this volume change.
distractorExplanations.B: This uses the volume change without dividing by the 2 cm H2O pressure change.
distractorExplanations.D: Multiplying volume change by pressure change is not compliance.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate static lung compliance from an equilibrated pressure-volume change.
