questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: In an isolated-lung experiment, substantially less transpulmonary pressure is needed to produce a given volume increase when the lung is filled with saline rather than air. What best explains this finding?

options.text: Saline removes all collagen and elastin from the lung
Saline strengthens the recoil produced by alveolar surface tension
Saline eliminates the alveolar air-fluid interface and its surface tension contribution
Saline causes the chest wall muscles to contract more strongly

questions.explanation: A saline-filled lung lacks the air-fluid interface responsible for much of the recoil of an air-filled lung. Tissue elasticity remains, but the surface tension contribution is removed.

distractorExplanations.A: Saline filling does not remove the lung's elastic tissue; tissue recoil is still present.
distractorExplanations.B: The surface tension contribution is removed, not strengthened, when there is no air-fluid interface.
distractorExplanations.D: This is an isolated lung; chest wall muscle activity cannot explain its pressure-volume relation.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish tissue elasticity from alveolar surface tension as sources of lung recoil.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A premature infant has inadequate pulmonary surfactant. Which change most directly explains the increased tendency of the alveoli to collapse?

options.text: Increased surface tension in the alveolar lining fluid
Decreased elastic recoil of the air-filled lungs
Increased ease of lung expansion at a given pressure
Loss of the normal surface-tension-raising action of surfactant

questions.explanation: Surfactant, secreted by type II alveolar epithelial cells, lowers surface tension. Its deficiency raises the surface tension force tending to collapse the alveoli and makes inflation more difficult.

distractorExplanations.B: Surfactant deficiency increases the surface tension component of recoil rather than decreasing it.
distractorExplanations.C: Deficiency makes expansion harder, not easier, for a given distending pressure.
distractorExplanations.D: Normal surfactant lowers surface tension; it does not raise it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how surfactant deficiency alters alveolar stability and inflation.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Two idealized spherical alveoli have identical, constant lining-fluid surface tension. Alveolus X has half the radius of alveolus Y. Using the book's relationship P = 2T/r, how does the pressure tending to collapse X compare with that for Y?

options.text: One-quarter as great
One-half as great
The same
Twice as great

questions.explanation: With surface tension held constant, collapse pressure is inversely proportional to radius. Halving the radius doubles 2T/r; real surfactant behavior is intentionally excluded by the stated assumption.

distractorExplanations.A: The stated relationship contains the first power of radius in the denominator, not its square.
distractorExplanations.B: Halving radius increases rather than decreases pressure when surface tension is unchanged.
distractorExplanations.C: Equal surface tension does not produce equal pressure when the radii differ.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the inverse relationship between alveolar radius and collapse pressure with surface tension fixed.

questions.subtopic: Work of breathing and airway resistance
questions.prompt: During an episode of bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, a patient must generate a larger pressure difference to maintain the same airflow. Which component of the work of inspiration is most directly increased?

options.text: Work required to overcome lung tissue elasticity alone
Airway resistance work
Work required to increase alveolar diffusion capacity
Work required to transport oxygen bound to hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Narrowing the airway increases resistance to airflow. The additional pressure needed to move air through that resistance increases airway resistance work.

distractorExplanations.A: Elastic work concerns expansion against recoil; the specified change is airway narrowing.
distractorExplanations.C: Diffusion across the respiratory membrane is not a mechanical work component of inspiration.
distractorExplanations.D: Hemoglobin transport is not one of the mechanical work components of breathing.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the work-of-breathing component increased by bronchoconstriction.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A student measures the volume of gas remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal, unforced expiration. Which volume or capacity has been measured?

options.text: Functional residual capacity
Residual volume
Inspiratory capacity
Vital capacity

questions.explanation: Functional residual capacity is the gas remaining after a normal expiration. It is the sum of expiratory reserve volume and residual volume.

distractorExplanations.B: Residual volume remains after the most forceful expiration, not merely a normal expiration.
distractorExplanations.C: Inspiratory capacity is the volume that can be inspired from the normal end-expiratory level.
distractorExplanations.D: Vital capacity is the maximum exhaled volume after maximal inspiration.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the definition and components of functional residual capacity.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Which quantity cannot be measured directly with a simple spirometer that records only air entering and leaving the mouth?

options.text: Tidal volume
Expiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Vital capacity

questions.explanation: Residual volume cannot be exhaled into the spirometer. Capacities containing residual volume also require another method, such as helium dilution, rather than simple spirometry alone.

distractorExplanations.A: Tidal volume is the inspired or expired volume of an ordinary breath and can be recorded.
distractorExplanations.B: Expiratory reserve volume is the extra volume exhaled after a normal expiration and can be recorded.
distractorExplanations.D: Vital capacity is an exhalable volume from maximal inspiration to maximal expiration and can be recorded.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish exhalable lung volumes from volumes inaccessible to simple spirometry.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A subject has a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1000 mL, and a residual volume of 1200 mL. What is the vital capacity?
questions.explanation: Vital capacity equals inspiratory reserve volume + tidal volume + expiratory reserve volume: 3000 + 500 + 1000 = 4500 mL. Residual volume is not included.

distractorExplanations.A: 3500 mL is the inspiratory capacity, which omits expiratory reserve volume.
distractorExplanations.C: 4700 mL incorrectly substitutes residual volume for expiratory reserve volume.
distractorExplanations.D: 5700 mL is total lung capacity, which includes residual volume.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate vital capacity and distinguish it from other lung capacities.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: At the end of a normal expiration, a subject is connected to a closed spirometer containing 3.0 L of gas with 10% helium. After complete mixing, helium concentration is 6%. Assume no leaks, negligible helium absorption, and correction for oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide removal. What is the functional residual capacity?
questions.explanation: FRC = initial spirometer volume x (initial helium fraction/final helium fraction - 1). Thus FRC = 3.0 x (10/6 - 1) = 2.0 L; the final combined gas volume is 5.0 L.

distractorExplanations.A: This does not conserve the initial helium quantity of 0.30 L across the combined volume.
distractorExplanations.B: Multiplying the fractional concentration fall by 3.0 L does not account for dilution into the added lung volume.
distractorExplanations.C: 5.0 L is the combined final volume of spirometer plus lung gas, not the lung volume alone.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate functional residual capacity using a closed-circuit helium dilution experiment.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A subject breathes 12 times/min with a tidal volume of 500 mL and a physiological dead space of 150 mL per breath. What is the alveolar ventilation?

options.text: 1.8 L/min
6.0 L/min
4.2 L/min
7.8 L/min

questions.explanation: Alveolar ventilation = respiratory rate x (tidal volume - physiological dead space). Therefore, 12 x (500 - 150) = 4200 mL/min = 4.2 L/min.

distractorExplanations.A: 1.8 L/min is dead-space ventilation: 12 x 150 mL.
distractorExplanations.B: 6.0 L/min is total minute ventilation and includes dead-space ventilation.
distractorExplanations.D: 7.8 L/min adds rather than subtracts dead-space volume from each tidal breath.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate alveolar ventilation after excluding physiological dead space.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A subject changes from 12 breaths/min at 500 mL per breath to 24 breaths/min at 250 mL per breath. Physiological dead space stays at 150 mL per breath. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Minute ventilation and alveolar ventilation both remain unchanged
Minute ventilation is unchanged, but alveolar ventilation falls from 4.2 to 2.4 L/min
Minute ventilation doubles, but alveolar ventilation is unchanged
Minute ventilation is unchanged, but alveolar ventilation rises from 4.2 to 6.0 L/min

questions.explanation: Minute ventilation is 6.0 L/min in both patterns. Alveolar ventilation falls from 12 x 350 = 4200 mL/min to 24 x 100 = 2400 mL/min because more breaths repeatedly ventilate dead space.

distractorExplanations.A: Equal minute ventilation does not imply equal alveolar ventilation when tidal volume and rate change.
distractorExplanations.C: Doubling rate while halving tidal volume leaves minute ventilation unchanged.
distractorExplanations.D: 6.0 L/min is the total minute ventilation; subtracting dead space gives only 2.4 L/min for the second pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Compare effective alveolar ventilation during deep-slow and shallow-rapid breathing.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
questions.prompt: A small group of alveoli becomes poorly ventilated, while ventilation elsewhere remains normal. What local vascular response helps improve the overall matching of pulmonary blood flow to ventilation?

options.text: Dilation of arteries supplying the hypoxic alveoli
Constriction of vessels supplying only the well-ventilated alveoli
Equal dilation of all pulmonary arterioles
Constriction of small pulmonary arteries supplying the hypoxic alveoli

questions.explanation: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary vasoconstriction. This diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward regions with better ventilation.

distractorExplanations.A: Dilation would direct more blood to poorly ventilated alveoli and worsen matching.
distractorExplanations.B: Constriction in well-ventilated regions would divert flow away from the regions best able to oxygenate it.
distractorExplanations.C: A uniform response would not selectively redirect blood away from the hypoxic region.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how local alveolar hypoxia redistributes pulmonary blood flow.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
questions.prompt: In a region of lung, alveolar pressure is 10 mm Hg. Local pulmonary arterial pressure varies from 15 mm Hg in systole to 5 mm Hg in diastole, and pulmonary venous pressure stays below 10 mm Hg. Which blood-flow pattern is expected?

options.text: Zone 2 flow: flow during systole but interruption during diastole
Zone 1 flow: no flow throughout the entire cardiac cycle
Zone 3 flow: continuous flow throughout the cardiac cycle
Continuous reverse flow from pulmonary veins to pulmonary arteries

questions.explanation: Arterial pressure exceeds alveolar pressure in systole but falls below it in diastole. This is zone 2, in which alveolar compression interrupts flow when intravascular pressure becomes too low.

distractorExplanations.B: Zone 1 requires alveolar pressure to exceed arterial pressure throughout the cycle, which is not true in systole here.
distractorExplanations.C: Continuous zone 3 flow requires vascular pressures to remain sufficient to prevent alveolar compression throughout the cycle.

Recruitment and distension of pulmonary capillaries
Diversion of most right ventricular output into the bronchial circulation
Generalized closure of upper-lung capillaries

questions.prompt: A sudden marked rise in left atrial pressure is followed by pulmonary interstitial edema. Assume that plasma protein concentration and capillary permeability have not initially changed. Which alteration most directly drives fluid out of the pulmonary capillaries?

Increased plasma colloid osmotic pressure
Decreased interstitial protein concentration
Decreased pulmonary capillary filtration pressure

A decrease in capillary permeability to protein
An isolated reduction in pulmonary venous pressure
Increased capillary permeability with leakage of protein and fluid

Conversion of the pulmonary circulation into a high-resistance circuit
Marked expansion of pulmonary lymphatic drainage capacity

questions.prompt: A person breathes air with an oxygen fraction of 0.21 at a barometric pressure of 500 mm Hg. Inspired gas becomes fully saturated with water vapor at 37 degrees C, where water vapor pressure is 47 mm Hg. Before alveolar gas exchange, what is the approximate oxygen partial pressure of this humidified inspired gas?

options.text: 58 mm Hg
105 mm Hg
95 mm Hg
149 mm Hg

questions.explanation: Water vapor occupies 47 mm Hg of the total pressure. Humidified inspired PO2 = 0.21 x (500 - 47) = 95.13 mm Hg, approximately 95 mm Hg; alveolar exchange is not included in this calculation.

distractorExplanations.A: This subtracts all 47 mm Hg from the dry oxygen partial pressure rather than applying oxygen fraction to the remaining dry-gas pressure.
distractorExplanations.B: 105 mm Hg is the dry-air oxygen partial pressure, 0.21 x 500, before humidification.

distractorExplanations.C: An increase in ventilation at fixed production lowers, rather than raises, alveolar PCO2.

questions.prompt: For a particular gas, respiratory membrane thickness doubles and available surface area falls to half its initial value. The diffusion coefficient and partial pressure difference remain unchanged. What fraction of the original diffusion rate is expected?

options.text: One-half
The same
Twice
One-quarter

questions.explanation: Diffusion rate is proportional to surface area and inversely proportional to thickness. The combined factor is (1/2)/2 = 1/4 of the original rate.

distractorExplanations.A: One-half accounts for either change alone but not both changes together.
distractorExplanations.B: Both changes reduce diffusion; they do not cancel one another.

questions.chapter: Chapter 40: Principles of Gas Exchange; Diffusion of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide Through Respiratory Membranes
questions.prompt: Under comparable conditions, carbon dioxide can cross the respiratory membrane at a much higher rate than oxygen for the same partial pressure difference. What chiefly explains this property?

options.text: Carbon dioxide has a lower molecular weight than oxygen
Carbon dioxide is much more soluble in the membrane and tissue fluid
Carbon dioxide requires no partial pressure difference to diffuse
Oxygen is unable to dissolve in the respiratory membrane

questions.explanation: The diffusion coefficient depends strongly on gas solubility and inversely on the square root of molecular weight. CO2's much greater solubility makes its diffusion rate about 20 times that of O2 for a given pressure difference.

distractorExplanations.A: CO2 has a higher, not lower, molecular weight; its greater solubility dominates this comparison.
distractorExplanations.C: Net CO2 diffusion still requires a partial pressure difference.
distractorExplanations.D: Oxygen does dissolve and diffuse through the membrane, but less readily than CO2 for the same pressure gradient.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the high diffusion coefficient of carbon dioxide relative to oxygen.

questions.prompt: Why is a small test concentration of carbon monoxide useful for measuring the lung's diffusing capacity?

options.text: Rapid binding to hemoglobin keeps capillary CO partial pressure nearly zero
CO cannot cross the respiratory membrane
CO is not taken up by pulmonary capillary blood
CO partial pressure immediately becomes equal on both sides of the membrane

questions.explanation: Rapid hemoglobin binding keeps capillary CO partial pressure close to zero during the test. The driving pressure can therefore be approximated by alveolar CO partial pressure, allowing uptake per unit pressure to be calculated.

distractorExplanations.B: CO must cross the membrane for its uptake to measure diffusing capacity.
distractorExplanations.C: Measured uptake into blood is essential to the method.
distractorExplanations.D: If partial pressures rapidly equalized, alveolar CO pressure alone would not represent the diffusion gradient.

PO2 104 mm Hg and PCO2 40 mm Hg
PO2 0 mm Hg and PCO2 0 mm Hg

questions.explanation: With ventilation absent and perfusion maintained, the V/Q ratio is zero. Alveolar gas equilibrates with the incoming venous blood rather than with inspired air.

questions.prompt: An embolus completely stops blood flow to an alveolar unit, but that unit remains ventilated with humidified room air at sea level. After sufficient time, what happens to its alveolar gases?

options.text: They approach mixed venous gas pressures
PO2 approaches inspired humidified-air PO2, and PCO2 approaches zero
PO2 falls to zero while PCO2 rises continuously
They necessarily remain at normal alveolar PO2 and PCO2

questions.explanation: With ventilation but no perfusion, V/Q approaches infinity. No blood removes O2 or delivers CO2, so the unit's gas approaches humidified inspired air; its ventilation is wasted for blood gas exchange.

distractorExplanations.A: Approach to venous gas pressures occurs when ventilation is absent and perfusion is maintained.
distractorExplanations.C: Without blood flow there is no continuing blood-borne oxygen removal or carbon dioxide delivery to cause this pattern.

questions.prompt: In a healthy upright person at rest, why is the ventilation-perfusion ratio generally higher at the lung apex than at the base?

Apical ventilation is greater than basal ventilation
Both are lower at the apex, but blood flow decreases proportionately more than ventilation
Gravity causes blood flow and ventilation to fall by exactly the same fraction

questions.prompt: A blood sample contains 10 g hemoglobin/dL, and hemoglobin is 90% saturated with oxygen. Assume each gram of hemoglobin binds 1.34 mL O2 at full saturation and ignore dissolved oxygen. What is its hemoglobin-bound oxygen content?

options.text: 9.0 mL O2/dL
12.1 mL O2/dL
13.4 mL O2/dL
20.1 mL O2/dL

questions.explanation: Bound oxygen content = hemoglobin concentration x oxygen capacity per gram x fractional saturation. Thus 10 x 1.34 x 0.90 = 12.06, or approximately 12.1 mL O2/dL.

distractorExplanations.A: Multiplying hemoglobin concentration by saturation alone omits its oxygen-binding capacity per gram.
distractorExplanations.C: 13.4 mL/dL is the capacity at 100% saturation, not the content at 90% saturation.
distractorExplanations.D: 20.1 mL/dL would be the full-saturation capacity of 15 g/dL hemoglobin, not the stated sample.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate hemoglobin-bound oxygen content from hemoglobin concentration and saturation.

questions.prompt: Arterial blood entering a tissue contains 20 mL O2/dL, and venous blood leaving it contains 15 mL O2/dL. Using oxygen content rather than partial pressure, what is the oxygen utilization coefficient?
questions.explanation: The tissue removes 20 - 15 = 5 mL O2/dL. The utilization coefficient is the fraction of delivered oxygen extracted: 5/20 x 100 = 25%.

distractorExplanations.B: 20 is the incoming oxygen content, not its extracted fraction.

questions.prompt: Why does a moderate fall in alveolar PO2 from about 104 to 60 mm Hg produce a relatively small fall in hemoglobin oxygen saturation, assuming normal hemoglobin and adequate equilibration?

options.text: Hemoglobin binds oxygen independently of oxygen partial pressure
Dissolved oxygen completely replaces hemoglobin-bound oxygen
This pressure range lies largely on the upper, relatively flat portion of the dissociation curve
Hemoglobin saturation rises whenever alveolar PO2 falls

questions.explanation: The upper part of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is relatively flat. Hemoglobin therefore remains substantially saturated despite a moderate reduction in alveolar and end-capillary PO2.

distractorExplanations.A: Oxygen binding depends on PO2; the small change reflects the curve's shape, not pressure independence.
distractorExplanations.B: Dissolved oxygen remains a small component under these conditions and does not replace hemoglobin carriage.
distractorExplanations.D: Saturation decreases as PO2 falls when the curve is otherwise unchanged.

questions.chapter: Chapter 41: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
questions.prompt: Blood passes through a metabolically active tissue where CO2 and hydrogen ion concentrations increase. At a given tissue PO2, how does this change affect hemoglobin?

options.text: It shifts the oxygen dissociation curve rightward and promotes oxygen release
It shifts the curve leftward and promotes oxygen release
It shifts the curve rightward and increases oxygen affinity
It leaves oxygen affinity unchanged because only PO2 can alter binding

questions.explanation: Increased CO2 and H+ shift the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right, reducing affinity at a given PO2 and enhancing unloading. This is the Bohr effect.

distractorExplanations.B: A left shift raises affinity and tends to impede unloading at a fixed PO2.
distractorExplanations.C: A right shift represents reduced, not increased, oxygen affinity.
distractorExplanations.D: CO2 and pH can alter affinity even when PO2 is held constant.

questions.prompt: Two blood samples have the same hemoglobin concentration, PO2, pH, PCO2, and 2,3-BPG concentration. One sample is warmed from 37 to 40 degrees C, as may occur locally in exercising muscle. What is expected in the warmed sample?

No change because temperature does not affect hemoglobin affinity
An increase in the maximum number of oxygen-binding sites per hemoglobin molecule
A right shift with greater tendency to release oxygen

distractorExplanations.B: Temperature is one of the factors that changes the curve independently of PO2.

questions.prompt: After sustained hypoxia, red-cell 2,3-BPG concentration rises. With other factors held constant, how does this change assist tissue oxygen delivery?

It converts most oxygen transport from the hemoglobin-bound to the dissolved form
It increases inspired oxygen partial pressure

CO increases the amount of oxygen that each hemoglobin molecule can carry

Bicarbonate leaves red cells while chloride enters

questions.prompt: During passage through pulmonary capillaries, oxygenation of hemoglobin promotes release of additional CO2. Which explanation describes the Haldane effect?

options.text: Oxygenation increases hemoglobin's capacity to bind CO2 and H+
A rise in CO2 shifts the oxygen dissociation curve rightward
Oxygenated hemoglobin binds less CO2 and releases H+, which helps convert bicarbonate into CO2
Oxygen directly replaces bicarbonate ions in the plasma

Phrenic motor fibers from the diaphragm to the spinal cord
Glossopharyngeal nerves from the carotid bodies

CO2 stimulates breathing mainly by raising arterial PO2
Central chemosensitive neurons are completely insensitive to H+
CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier readily and generates H+ in brain extracellular fluid and cerebrospinal fluid

Failure of CO2 to cross the blood-brain barrier after the first day

questions.prompt: A patient with markedly slow circulation develops repeating cycles of gradually deeper breathing followed by gradually shallower breathing or apnea. How can the prolonged circulation time promote this Cheyne-Stokes pattern?

It delays delivery of changed blood gases to the respiratory center, allowing corrective ventilation to overshoot
It makes the respiratory center respond before gas changes occur in the lungs
It removes the effect of carbon dioxide on respiratory neurons permanently
